the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: A small last addition that triggers collapse is the straw. The thin end of the wedge would be the first small step, not the last.

idioms.idiom: Put the cart before the horse
idioms.meaning: To do things in the wrong order
idioms.origin: The image goes back at least to Roman writing and has meant reversed logic in English since the 1500s.
idioms.caption: Right parts. Wrong order.

cards.q: They designed the brochure before deciding what the course would actually teach. The director said they had put the cart before the horse, meaning they had ___.
o: Done things in the wrong order
Spent money they did not yet have
Copied a rival's approach too closely
Planned far more than they could deliver
cards.why: The idiom is purely about sequence: the thing that should come second was done first.

cards.q: He booked the hall and printed the tickets before the artist had agreed to come at all. He had ___.
o: put the cart before the horse
cards.why: Doing the later step first is putting the cart before the horse. Gilding the lily is overdecorating something already fine.

words.meaning: Fussing too much over small rules and details, often to show off learning
words.note: From pedant, which once simply meant a schoolmaster.

cards.q: He corrected the speaker's Latin plurals in the middle of a eulogy, which everyone found painfully ___.
cards.why: Correcting grammar at a funeral is fussing over trivial rules. Generous, spontaneous and eloquent are all compliments that clash with 'painfully'.

o: Her pedantic notes on my essay fixed every comma but ignored the argument.
The pedantic host let the guests sit wherever they liked and skipped the speeches.
His pedantic account was loose and casual, full of happy guesses about the dates.
A pedantic editor rarely bothers with spelling, grammar or any of the small details.
cards.why: Pedantic means fussing over small rules, so relaxed seating, happy guesses and ignoring details all contradict it.

words.meaning: Looking or sounding sad and gloomy, often exaggeratedly so
words.note: Latin lugere = to mourn.

cards.q: The ___ tune from the old organ made the empty hall feel even colder.
cards.why: A mournful tune makes a hall feel colder. Lucrative means profitable, ludicrous means absurd, luminescent means glowing.

cards.q: A comedian delivers every joke with a long face and a slow, sorrowful voice, as if reading at a funeral. His manner is ___.
cards.why: A slow, sorrowful, funeral-like manner is lugubrious. Exuberant is lively, flippant is lightly dismissive, effervescent is bubbly.

words.meaning: Lazy; avoiding effort
words.note: Latin in- (not) + dolere (to feel pain): someone who will not trouble himself.

cards.q: The ___ clerk let the files pile up for weeks rather than open a single drawer.
cards.why: Letting files pile up rather than lift a finger is laziness. Diligent is the opposite, anxious is worried, frugal is careful with money.

o: After the exams he wanted nothing more than one indolent week by the sea.
The indolent farmer was out before dawn and in the fields until it was dark.
Her indolent habits had her finishing every assignment a whole week early.
He was so indolent that he volunteered for every extra shift that came up.
cards.why: Indolent means lazy, so working dawn to dusk, finishing early and volunteering for extra shifts all contradict it.

words.meaning: Showing intense, passionate feeling
words.note: Latin fervere = to boil, as in fervour and effervescent.

o: She was a fervent supporter of the club and never missed a home match.
His fervent interest in the subject lasted about as long as a single lecture.
With fervent indifference, he shrugged and turned back to his phone again.
The fervent crowd sat in silence, barely noticing the players on the field.
cards.why: Fervent means burning with feeling, so a short-lived interest, indifference and a silent crowd all contradict it.

cards.q: A student writes to the principal every week, campaigns door to door and speaks at every meeting to save the school library. Her support is ___.
cards.why: Weekly letters and door-to-door campaigning show intense passion. Lukewarm is half-hearted, nominal is in name only, grudging is reluctant.

words.meaning: Kindly and well-meaning; wanting to do good
words.note: Latin bene (well) + volens (wishing). Its opposite is malevolent.

cards.q: The ___ trust paid the fees of every girl in the village who passed the entrance exam.
cards.why: Paying girls' fees is wishing them well. Malevolent wishes harm, belligerent is hostile, ambivalent is undecided.

cards.q: Under the gruff manner was a ___ man who quietly paid his staff's hospital bills.
cards.why: 'Under the gruff manner' sets up a kind heart, proved by the bills. Vindictive, miserly and callous all agree with the gruffness instead.

idioms.meaning: To suffer a final, decisive defeat
idioms.origin: Napoleon's last battle, lost at Waterloo in Belgium in 1815 after years of victories.
idioms.caption: Years unbeaten. Then one field in Belgium.

cards.q: The champion had not lost a match in three years, but he met his Waterloo against an unseeded teenager. He ___.
o: Played below his usual level for a day
Lost because of an unfair umpiring call
Retired at the very peak of his career
cards.why: Waterloo is not just any loss: it ends a long winning run, decisively.

cards.q: The chain had seen off every rival for a decade, until a small online start-up took its market and forced it to close. The chain had ___.
cards.why: A final defeat after a long run is meeting one's Waterloo. Crossing the Rubicon and burning one's boats are about committing, not losing.

idioms.meaning: To act in a way that makes retreat impossible, committing yourself fully
idioms.origin: Invading commanders, from ancient times on, are said to have burned their own ships so their soldiers could not turn back.
idioms.caption: No way back. Only forward.

cards.q: He resigned from the bank and sold his flat to fund the restaurant, burning his boats. He had ___.
o: Left himself no way back to his old life
Wasted all his savings on a reckless gamble
Cut every tie with his family and his friends
Ignored the advice of people who knew better
cards.why: The idiom is about removing the way back, not about whether the risk was wise.

cards.q: She turned down the scholarship abroad and told the university she would not be coming, so the start-up was now her only option. She had ___.
cards.why: Removing your own fallback is burning your boats. Hedging your bets is the opposite: keeping options open.

words.meaning: To persuade someone by flattery or gentle coaxing
words.note: From French cajoler, to chatter like a jay, and so to coax.

cards.q: She managed to ___ her grandfather into trying the phone by promising he could video-call his brother.
cards.why: A tempting promise is coaxing. Coerce means force, dismiss means brush aside, deride means mock.

cards.q: No amount of threats would move him, but a little flattery was enough to ___ him into signing.
cards.why: The contrast with threats points to gentle persuasion. Cudgel means beat, console means comfort in grief, cripple means disable.

words.meaning: Bitter, long-lasting resentment
words.note: Latin rancor = rankness, rancidness, the same root as rancid.

o: Years after the split, he still spoke of his old partner with real rancour.
With warm rancour, she thanked him for all the help he had given her that year.
Their rancour showed in how gladly they shared the prize and hugged on stage.
There was no hint of rancour between them, so they refused to speak for a decade.
cards.why: Rancour is lasting bitterness, so warm thanks and glad hugs contradict it, and 'no rancour' cannot explain ten years of silence.

cards.q: She lost the election narrowly but congratulated her rival without a trace of ___.
cards.why: 'Without a trace of' needs something bad to be absent: bitterness. Humility, grace and warmth would be expected in a gracious loser.

words.meaning: To praise highly, especially in public
words.note: Latin laus = praise, the root of laudable and applaud.

cards.q: Critics ___ the novel for its honesty, though few readers made it past the first hundred pages.
cards.why: The 'though' contrasts critical praise with poor reading. Panned and ignored would not need a contrast, and banned does not fit critics.

o: The minister lauded the volunteers for clearing the flooded streets so quickly.
The coach lauded the team so harshly that two players asked to be transferred.
Reviewers lauded the film as a dull, careless mess they would never sit through again.
He lauded her in private, telling no one at all how highly he really thought of her.
cards.why: Laud means praise, usually openly, so harsh words, a damning review and private silence all contradict it.

words.meaning: A person who lives alone and avoids company
words.note: Latin recludere = to shut away.

cards.q: A famous novelist has not given an interview in thirty years, lives behind high gates and sends his groceries in by van. He is a ___.
cards.why: Shutting oneself away for decades is what a recluse does. A socialite and a raconteur thrive on company; celebrity describes fame, not avoidance.

cards.q: After the scandal he became a ___, leaving the house only at night.
cards.why: A person who hides away is a recluse. A refuge is a place of safety, a recruit is a new member, a rebuke is a scolding.

words.meaning: Full of intense, sometimes excessive enthusiasm for a cause
words.note: From zeal; the Zealots were a first-century movement known for their fierce devotion.

cards.q: The new inspector was so ___ that he fined a stall for a sign that was two centimetres too wide.
cards.why: Fining someone over two centimetres is over-eager enforcement. Lenient, negligent and indifferent all mean the opposite.

o: A zealous convert to running, he now talks about nothing but his marathon times.
The zealous volunteers drifted away within a week, barely noticed by anyone.
She was zealous about the cause, shrugging whenever anyone happened to bring it up.
His zealous approach to the rules meant he simply ignored the ones he disliked.
cards.why: Zealous means burning enthusiasm, so drifting away, shrugging and ignoring rules all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: The largest part of something
idioms.origin: From Aesop's fable in which the lion, hunting with other animals, claims every part of the kill for itself.
idioms.caption: One quarter each. Then the lion did the counting.

cards.q: The founder kept the lion's share of the profits, paying the other two partners very little. He kept ___.
o: A secret portion nobody knew of
The portion he had been promised
cards.why: The lion's share is simply the largest part, usually more than is fair.

cards.q: Out of a budget of ten crore, eight went to the stadium and two were split among all the other projects. The stadium got ___.
cards.why: Eight out of ten is the largest part: the lion's share. A white elephant is a costly, useless possession.

idioms.meaning: Someone dangerous who pretends to be harmless
idioms.origin: From the Sermon on the Mount, which warns against false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are wolves within.
idioms.caption: Soft wool. Sharp teeth.

cards.q: The friendly advisor who offered to manage the widow's savings turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing. He was ___.
o: A predator hiding behind a harmless manner
An honest man who made an innocent mistake
A clumsy fraud everyone saw through at once
A strict man with a surprisingly kind heart
cards.why: The idiom joins two things: real danger and a gentle disguise. The last option reverses it.

cards.q: The charming new tenant who offered to help with everyone's bills was quietly copying their bank details. He was ___.
cards.why: Danger behind a harmless face is a wolf in sheep's clothing. A paper tiger is the reverse: it looks dangerous but is not.

words.meaning: Acting with care and thought for the future
words.note: Latin prudens, a contraction of providens, seeing ahead.

cards.q: With a monsoon forecast, it seemed ___ to move the books from the ground floor before the weekend.
cards.why: Acting before a forecast storm is careful foresight. Reckless and impulsive are the opposite, and futile means pointless.

cards.q: A woman who has just won a large sum pays off her loan, saves half and keeps working while she decides what to do with the rest. Her approach is ___.
cards.why: Paying debts and saving show careful thought for the future. Profligate is wasteful, quixotic is impractically idealistic, impetuous is rash.

words.meaning: Lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern
words.note: Greek a- (without) + pathos (feeling).

o: Voter apathy was so deep that fewer than a third of residents turned up.
Their apathy showed in the hundreds of letters they sent to the council.
Out of sheer apathy he campaigned in every ward, night after night.
Her apathy for the cause kept her awake most nights, drafting new plans.
cards.why: Apathy means not caring, so hundreds of letters, nightly campaigning and sleepless planning all contradict it.

cards.q: The teacher could handle disagreement; what she could not bear was the class's ___.
cards.why: The contrast with disagreement points to not caring at all. Curiosity, diligence and enthusiasm are things a teacher would welcome.

words.meaning: Showing a cruel lack of concern for others
words.note: Latin callosus = hard-skinned, the root of callus; a callous heart has hardened.

cards.q: Laughing at the accident victim was a ___ thing to do.
cards.why: Laughing at a victim is unfeeling. Callow means young and inexperienced, cautious means careful, copious means plentiful.

o: It was callous of him to cancel her leave on the day of her father's funeral.
Her callous words to the grieving family brought them real comfort that night.
The callous nurse sat up all night holding the frightened patient's hand.
He was so callous that he wept openly at every sad story he heard.
cards.why: Callous means hard-hearted, so bringing comfort, sitting up with a patient and weeping all contradict it.

words.meaning: Fluent and persuasive in speech or writing
words.note: Latin eloqui = to speak out.

cards.q: Her speech was so ___ that even those who disagreed with her rose to applaud.
cards.why: Winning over opponents takes persuasive fluency. Halting, tedious and incoherent would not bring them to their feet.

cards.q: A man says nothing at the protest. He simply holds up the photograph of his drowned son, and the crowd falls silent. His silence was ___.
cards.why: Eloquent can describe anything that expresses a lot, even silence. Garrulous means talkative, evasive avoids the point, pedantic fusses over small rules.

words.meaning: Irresponsible and lacking any sense of purpose
words.note: Scots feck = effect, value; feckless = without effect.

cards.q: Her ___ brother had borrowed money from every relative and repaid none of it.
cards.why: Borrowing from all and repaying nothing is irresponsibility. Diligent, frugal and scrupulous are all virtues.

o: The feckless manager missed the deadline, blamed the intern and went on leave.
A feckless planner, she had every detail of the trip booked months in advance.
He was feckless with money, saving a fixed share of his salary every month.
The feckless captain kept the team focused, calm and disciplined all season.
cards.why: Feckless means irresponsible and aimless, so careful booking, steady saving and disciplined captaincy all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: Excessively harsh or severe, usually of laws or punishments
idioms.origin: Draco, a lawgiver in ancient Athens, prescribed death for even minor crimes; his laws were said to be written in blood.
idioms.caption: Steal a cabbage? Death.

cards.q: The draconian new rules expel a student for a single late assignment. The rules are ___.
o: Far harsher than the offence deserves
Strict, but fair and clearly explained
cards.why: Draconian means punishment out of all proportion to the offence.

cards.q: The society fined residents five thousand rupees for leaving a shoe outside the door. The fine was ___.
cards.why: A punishment wildly out of proportion is draconian. Procrustean means forcing things to fit a rigid standard.

idioms.meaning: To raise a false alarm so often that real warnings are ignored
idioms.origin: From Aesop's fable of the shepherd boy who called 'Wolf!' for fun, so no one came when a wolf really appeared.
idioms.caption: Third time, nobody came.

cards.q: He had cried wolf about chest pain so many times that, when it was real, his family waited before calling a doctor. He had ___.
o: Raised false alarms until no one believed him
Been too proud to ask anyone for help in time
Hidden a serious illness from his whole family
Exaggerated a small problem to win sympathy once
cards.why: The point of the idiom is repetition: false alarms wear out belief in the true one.

cards.q: The app sent 'urgent' alerts every hour for trivial updates, so users ignored the one that warned of a real data breach. The app had ___.
cards.why: Repeated false alarms that kill trust are crying wolf. Gilding the lily is over-decorating what is already fine.

words.meaning: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to a fall
words.note: Greek hybris; in Greek tragedy, the arrogance that invites the gods' punishment.

cards.q: It was pure ___ to announce the victory parade before a single vote had been counted.
cards.why: Planning a parade before the count is overconfidence. Humility, prudence and diffidence are all forms of restraint.

cards.q: A ship's owner boasts that his vessel is unsinkable, carries too few lifeboats and orders full speed through an ice field. His attitude shows ___.
cards.why: Arrogant overconfidence that invites disaster is hubris. Apathy is not caring, rancour is bitterness, clemency is mercy.

words.meaning: Acting quickly without thinking or care
words.note: Latin impetus = attack, rush.

cards.q: In an ___ moment he quit his job by text, then spent the evening asking for it back.
cards.why: Quitting by text and regretting it hours later is rash. Impervious means unaffected, imperious means bossy, impeccable means flawless.

o: An impetuous decision to buy the car left him with a loan he could not afford.
After months of careful thought, she made the impetuous choice to move abroad.
His impetuous planning covered every possibility over the course of a full year.
The impetuous judge weighed each argument slowly before reaching a decision.
cards.why: Impetuous means acting on impulse, so months of thought, a year of planning and slow weighing all contradict it.

words.meaning: To throw away or abandon something no longer wanted
words.note: Originally throwing cargo overboard to lighten a ship; related to jetsam.

cards.q: To save the budget, the board had to ___ the plan for a second campus.
cards.why: Saving money by dropping a plan is jettisoning it. Finance, expand and announce would all cost more.

o: The pilot jettisoned fuel over the sea before the emergency landing.
The party jettisoned its old slogan by printing it on every new poster.
She jettisoned her notes carefully, filing each one in its proper folder.
He jettisoned the old car by giving it a fresh coat of paint and new tyres.
cards.why: To jettison is to throw away, so printing, filing and repainting all keep the thing instead.

words.meaning: No longer produced or used; out of date
words.note: Latin obsolescere = to grow old, fall into disuse.

cards.q: Streaming made the video rental shop ___ almost overnight.
cards.why: A new technology replacing an old business makes it out of date. Popular, profitable and essential suggest the reverse.

cards.q: A ministry still requires forms to be submitted by fax, though no office has owned a fax machine in years. The rule is ___.
cards.why: A rule for technology nobody uses is out of date. Nascent means just beginning, pertinent means relevant, ubiquitous means everywhere.

words.meaning: To regard with great respect and reverence
words.note: Latin venerari = to worship, revere.

cards.q: Villagers still ___ the old teacher who taught three generations to read.
cards.why: Deep respect for a beloved teacher is veneration. Venture means dare, ventilate means air out, vindicate means clear of blame.

o: Generations of musicians venerate the old master and play his songs.
The fans venerated the striker by booing him off the field after every match.
She venerated her mentor so much that she never once mentioned his name.
They venerate the founder and are trying to have his statue quietly taken down.
cards.why: Venerate means revere, so booing, ignoring and removing a statue all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: Careful about small sums but wasteful with large ones
idioms.origin: An English proverb from the 1600s, when the pound and penny were the units of daily life.
idioms.caption: Saved a rupee. Lost a lakh.

cards.q: Skipping the ten-rupee service to save money and then paying for a new engine is penny wise, pound foolish. It means ___.
o: Saving small sums at the cost of big ones
Being careful with every rupee you spend
Spending freely on the things that matter
Losing money through pure bad luck
cards.why: The idiom is about a false economy: thrift on small things causing large losses.

cards.q: The company cut the security budget to save a few lakh and then lost crores in a data breach. The decision was ___.
o: throwing the baby out with the bathwater
cards.why: Small savings that cause a huge loss are penny wise, pound foolish. A Pyrrhic victory is a win that costs too much.

idioms.meaning: To avoid stirring up an old problem that is currently quiet
idioms.origin: Recorded in Chaucer in the 1300s: a sleeping dog is harmless, so do not wake it.
idioms.caption: Quiet now. Keep it that way.

cards.q: She thought of raising the old property quarrel at dinner, but decided to let sleeping dogs lie. She decided ___.
o: Not to revive a quarrel that had faded
To settle the quarrel once and for all
To let her brother win the old argument
To raise it later, when the time was right
cards.why: The idiom recommends leaving a dormant trouble alone, not settling or postponing it.

cards.q: The auditor found a tiny error from ten years ago that had harmed no one. Her manager advised her to ___.
o: beard the lion in its den
cards.why: Leaving a harmless old issue undisturbed is letting sleeping dogs lie. Grasping the nettle is the opposite: tackling it head-on.

words.meaning: To become less intense or widespread
words.note: Old French abatre = to beat down.

cards.q: The ferries stayed in port until the storm began to ___.
cards.why: Ferries wait for a storm to weaken. Intensify, gather and erupt all mean it is getting worse.

o: The fever abated overnight and by morning she was asking for breakfast.
The noise abated until it was too loud for anyone to hear the speaker.
Public anger abated as more and more people joined the protests each day.
The flood abated so fast that whole villages were swept away by the evening.
cards.why: Abate means lessen, so growing louder, swelling protests and sweeping floods all contradict it.

words.meaning: Abrupt and short in manner, to the point of rudeness
words.note: Italian brusco = sour, tart.

cards.q: His ___ reply, 'Not now,' left the new intern unsure whether to stay or leave.
cards.why: Two curt words that leave someone unsure are abrupt. Courteous is polite, effusive is gushing, verbose is wordy.

cards.q: A doctor answers every question in three words, never looks up from the file and ends each visit by opening the door. Her manner is ___.
cards.why: Short answers and an open door are abrupt. Solicitous means caring, garrulous means chatty, obsequious means fawning.

words.meaning: A harsh, jarring mixture of sounds
words.note: Greek kakos (bad) + phone (sound). Its opposite is euphony.

cards.q: Horns, drills and a wedding band combined in a ___ outside the exam hall.
cards.why: Horns, drills and a band together make a jarring noise. Symphony and harmony are pleasing, tranquillity is calm and quiet.

o: The station was a cacophony of announcements, whistles and shouting porters.
A gentle cacophony of birdsong drifted softly across the silent lake at dawn.
The choir's cacophony was so perfectly blended that the audience wept.
In the cacophony of the empty library, she could hear a single page turn.
cards.why: A cacophony is harsh, jarring noise, so gentle birdsong, perfect blending and a silent library all contradict it.

words.meaning: Insisting that one's beliefs are true without considering evidence or other views
words.note: Greek dogma = opinion, decree.

cards.q: He is so ___ about his diet that he dismisses every study that disagrees with him.
cards.why: Dismissing all contrary evidence is rigid certainty. Open-minded and tentative are flexible, and sceptical means doubting, not insisting.

o: Her dogmatic insistence on one method left no room for anyone's experiments.
A dogmatic thinker, he changed his mind whenever someone offered good evidence.
The dogmatic professor encouraged students to challenge all his theories freely.
His dogmatic views were loosely held and easily set aside in any argument.
cards.why: Dogmatic means fixed and closed to evidence, so changing one's mind, inviting challenge and loosely held views all contradict it.

words.meaning: A mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh or blunt one
words.note: Greek eu (well) + pheme (speaking).

cards.q: A company announces that 400 employees have been 'released to pursue other opportunities'. That phrase is a ___.
cards.why: A gentle phrase standing in for 'sacked' is a euphemism. A paradox is a self-contradiction, hyperbole is exaggeration, a eulogy praises the dead.

cards.q: 'Passed away' is a common ___ for 'died'.
cards.why: A softer word for a harsh one is a euphemism. Euphoria is intense happiness, a euphonium is a brass instrument, euphony is pleasing sound.

idioms.meaning: The ability to make money or succeed in everything one attempts
idioms.origin: King Midas of Greek myth was granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, including, to his horror, his food.
idioms.caption: Everything he touched, golden.

cards.q: Every business the investor backed became a success; people said he had the Midas touch. He ___.
o: Made a success of every venture
Was born into a very wealthy family
Spent his fortune on gold and jewellery
Was greedy and cared only about money
cards.why: In everyday use the idiom means a knack for success, not greed.

cards.q: Her first three restaurants were hits, and now even her food truck has a two-hour queue. She seems to have ___.
cards.why: Success at everything is the Midas touch. Feet of clay is a hidden flaw in someone admired.

idioms.meaning: To offer something valuable to people who cannot appreciate it
idioms.origin: From the Sermon on the Mount: 'neither cast ye your pearls before swine'.
idioms.caption: Pearls. Pigs. Wrong audience.

cards.q: Reading his finest poem to a room watching cricket felt like casting pearls before swine. It felt like ___.
o: Giving something fine to those who could not value it
Wasting a great deal of time on something of little worth
Showing off in front of an audience he secretly disliked
Giving away something precious he would later regret
cards.why: The idiom joins a valuable gift with an audience unable to appreciate it.

cards.q: The chef served a rare truffle dish at a party where guests only wanted to know when the pizza was arriving. He had ___.
o: killed the goose that lays the golden eggs
cards.why: A fine thing wasted on an unappreciative audience is casting pearls before swine. Carrying coals to Newcastle is bringing something to where it is already plentiful.

words.meaning: Treating serious matters with inappropriate humour
words.note: Latin facetia = a jest.

cards.q: When asked how he would fix the deficit, he made a ___ remark about selling the Taj Mahal.
cards.why: A joke in reply to a serious question is facetious. Sanctimonious is self-righteous, cogent is convincing, candid is frank.

o: Her facetious comment about the fire drill annoyed the safety officer.
His facetious answer was so grave and careful that the panel nodded slowly.
The facetious eulogy kept every mourner in respectful, tearful silence.
With a facetious frown, the judge solemnly read out the long sentence.
cards.why: Facetious means joking at the wrong time, so grave care, respectful silence and a solemn reading all contradict it.

words.meaning: Obtrusively bright and showy
words.note: Origin uncertain; possibly from an old verb gaure, to stare.

cards.q: The ___ neon sign looked out of place on the quiet heritage street.
cards.why: Neon that clashes with a heritage street is loud and showy. Subtle, muted and elegant would blend in.

cards.q: She wore a ___ orange-and-purple suit that could be seen from across the stadium.
cards.why: Bright, clashing colours are garish. Garrulous means talkative, gracious means courteous, ghastly means horrifying.

words.meaning: A long, loud, aggressive speech; to lecture someone in this way
words.note: Old Italian aringa = a speech made in a public square.

cards.q: For forty minutes the coach paced the dressing room, shouting at each player in turn about their mistakes. He delivered a ___.
cards.why: A long, loud, angry lecture is a harangue. A eulogy praises the dead, a whisper is quiet, a compliment is praise.

o: The passenger harangued the driver all the way from the airport to the hotel.
She harangued the crowd in a soft, brief whisper that only the front row heard.
His harangue lasted a single sentence and was full of warm, gentle praise.
The minister harangued reporters by politely thanking them for their questions.
cards.why: A harangue is long, loud and aggressive, so a soft whisper, a gentle sentence and polite thanks all contradict it.

words.meaning: A habit or way of behaving peculiar to one person
words.note: Greek idios (own) + synkrasis (mixture): one's own blend of temperament.

cards.q: One of the professor's ___ was refusing to start a lecture until every window was open.
cards.why: A personal odd habit is an idiosyncrasy. Responsibilities are duties, ambitions are goals, grievances are complaints.

cards.q: A famous batsman always taps his bat three times, touches his helmet and looks at the sky before every ball. These rituals are his ___.
cards.why: Personal quirks like these are idiosyncrasies. Statistics are figures, credentials are qualifications, accomplishments are achievements.

words.meaning: To place side by side, especially to show contrast
words.note: Latin juxta (next to) + French poser (to place).

cards.q: The exhibition ___ photographs of the river in 1950 and today, so the damage speaks for itself.
cards.why: Putting then-and-now photos together to show contrast is juxtaposing. Conceals hides, exaggerates overstates, replaces swaps.

o: The film juxtaposes a lavish wedding with the slum just outside its gates.
She juxtaposed the two reports by locking one away so no one could compare them.
The designer juxtaposed the colours by using only a single shade of grey.
He juxtaposed the ideas by keeping them in separate books, years apart.
cards.why: To juxtapose is to put things side by side, so locking one away, using a single shade and keeping them apart all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: To celebrate lavishly, especially to welcome someone back
idioms.origin: From the parable of the Prodigal Son, whose father orders the fatted calf killed for a feast when his wayward son returns.
idioms.caption: He came home. Out came the feast.

cards.q: When their son returned after five years abroad, his parents killed the fatted calf. They ___.
o: Threw a lavish party to welcome him back
Scolded him for having stayed away so long
Asked him to repay the money he had borrowed
Quietly carried on with their normal routine
cards.why: The idiom means a generous welcome-home celebration.

cards.q: When the star coach rejoined the academy, the owners threw a grand dinner and hung banners across the gate. They ___.
cards.why: A lavish welcome for a returner is killing the fatted calf. Resting on one's laurels is coasting on past success.

idioms.meaning: A state of privileged detachment from the practical realities of life
idioms.origin: Originally a biblical image of purity; by the 1800s it described artists and scholars shut away from ordinary life.
idioms.caption: Lovely view. Far from the ground.

cards.q: Critics said the economist's plan was written from an ivory tower. They meant he was ___.
o: Out of touch with real people's lives
Too ambitious for a government to afford
Hiding the true cost of his proposal
cards.why: An ivory tower is detachment from real life, typically of academics or experts.

cards.q: The committee designing the farm policy had never once visited a village or spoken to a farmer. They were working from ___.
cards.why: Remote theorising without contact with reality is an ivory tower. A Potemkin village is a fake show of prosperity.

words.meaning: Clear and easy to understand
words.note: Latin lucidus = bright, from lux, light.

cards.q: After pages of jargon, her ___ summary was a relief: three sentences, and everyone understood.
cards.why: Three sentences everyone understands is clarity. Convoluted, cryptic and verbose all make understanding harder.

o: The surgeon gave a lucid explanation using a simple drawing.
His lucid instructions left the whole team confused about what to do next.
The lucid report was so tangled that no one could follow its argument.
She wrote a lucid paragraph that even its own author could not understand.
cards.why: Lucid means clear, so confusion, tangled argument and incomprehensibility all contradict it.

words.meaning: Lacking foresight; short-sighted
words.note: Greek myops = short-sighted, literally 'shutting the eyes'.

cards.q: Cutting the research budget to boost this quarter's profit was a ___ decision.
cards.why: Sacrificing the future for one quarter is short-sighted. Visionary, prudent and far-sighted are the opposite.

cards.q: A town cuts down its only forest to build a car park, then floods every monsoon because nothing holds the soil. The planning was ___.
cards.why: Ignoring the long-term cost is short-sighted. Meticulous means very careful, nascent means just beginning, lucid means clear.

words.meaning: Just beginning to exist or develop
words.note: Latin nasci = to be born, as in nation and native.

cards.q: The ___ start-up had three employees and one office chair.
cards.why: Three employees and one chair is a business just starting out. Established, declining and venerable all describe older things.

cards.q: Her ___ interest in photography grew into a career within five years.
cards.why: An interest just starting to develop is nascent. Nauseous means sick, nasal relates to the nose, noxious means harmful.

words.meaning: Giving the impression that something bad is about to happen
words.note: Latin omen = a sign of what is to come.

cards.q: The ___ silence from the examiner's room made the students fear the worst.
cards.why: A silence that makes people fear the worst is ominous. Reassuring, cheerful and festive suggest good news.

o: Dark clouds gathered in an ominous line along the horizon.
The ominous news that she had topped the exam made the whole family celebrate.
An ominous ray of sunshine promised a perfect day at the beach.
His ominous smile told her at once that everything was going to be fine.
cards.why: Ominous signals coming trouble, so good news, a perfect day and reassurance all contradict it.

words.meaning: Deep in serious, often sad thought
words.note: French penser = to think.

cards.q: He sat ___ by the window, turning the old letter over and over in his hands.
cards.why: Quietly turning a letter over is deep thought. Boisterous is noisy, frivolous is not serious, jubilant is joyful.

cards.q: After the result, the captain sits alone on the boundary rope for an hour, staring at the pitch and saying nothing. His mood is ___.
cards.why: Silent, serious reflection is pensive. Exuberant is lively, facetious is joking, brusque is curt.

idioms.meaning: Cunning, scheming and unscrupulous in pursuit of power
idioms.origin: From Niccolò Machiavelli, whose 1513 book The Prince advised rulers that the ends can justify ruthless means.
idioms.caption: Smile in public. Move pieces in private.

cards.q: The deputy's Machiavellian manoeuvres, leaking rumours and playing rivals against each other, won him the top job. They were ___.
o: Honest efforts that happened to succeed
Clumsy plots that everyone saw through
cards.why: Machiavellian joins cunning with a willingness to use unscrupulous means.

cards.q: She befriended both candidates, fed each false stories about the other, and stepped in as the compromise choice when they fell out. Her strategy was ___.
cards.why: Manipulating rivals to gain power is Machiavellian. Quixotic is impractically idealistic.

idioms.meaning: A custom, word or belief that marks out a group, often an outdated one
idioms.origin: In the Book of Judges, soldiers identified enemies by whether they could pronounce the Hebrew word shibboleth.
idioms.caption: Say it right, and you are one of us.

cards.q: 'Never borrow money' had become a shibboleth in the family, repeated without anyone asking whether it still made sense. It had become ___.
o: A belief repeated as a mark of belonging
A rule that was strictly enforced by law
A secret that only the eldest knew
A joke that nobody took seriously
cards.why: A shibboleth marks group belonging, and often survives after its sense is forgotten.

cards.q: Using the right slang was how the club's old members recognised each other, and newcomers who got it wrong were quietly frozen out. The slang was ___.
cards.why: A word that marks insiders from outsiders is a shibboleth. A red herring is a deliberate distraction.

words.meaning: Calm and not easily upset
words.note: Latin placidus = gentle, from placere, to please.

cards.q: Even when the flight dropped sharply, the ___ old man simply turned the page of his newspaper.
cards.why: Turning a page during turbulence shows calm. Frantic, agitated and hysterical all describe panic.

cards.q: The ___ surface of the lake showed every reflection perfectly.
cards.why: A still, calm lake is placid. Flaccid means limp, placated means soothed after anger, plausible means believable.

words.meaning: A cancellation or postponement of a punishment or a threat; to grant one
words.note: Old French repris, taken back.

cards.q: The old cinema won a last-minute ___ when a trust bought it a week before demolition.
cards.why: Being saved just before demolition is a reprieve. A verdict is a decision, a penalty is a punishment, an eviction is a removal.

o: The rain gave the farmers a brief reprieve from the long, punishing drought.
The court's reprieve sent him straight to prison two weeks earlier than planned.
As a reprieve, the teacher doubled the homework and cancelled the holiday.
The factory won a reprieve when the owners shut it down the very next morning.
cards.why: A reprieve postpones or cancels something bad, so earlier prison, doubled homework and an immediate shutdown all contradict it.

words.meaning: To satisfy fully, or more than fully
words.note: Latin satis = enough, as in satisfy.

cards.q: No number of followers could ___ his hunger for attention.
cards.why: A hunger that can never be filled cannot be satiated. Stimulate would increase it, measure and disguise do not fit hunger.

cards.q: After the twelve-course wedding lunch, the guests could not face even a sweet. They were ___.
cards.why: Too full to eat more is satiated. Famished and ravenous mean very hungry, peckish means slightly hungry.

words.meaning: Real and able to be seen, touched or measured
words.note: Latin tangere = to touch, as in tangent and contact.

cards.q: After a year of promises, residents wanted ___ results: repaired roads, not more speeches.
cards.why: Repaired roads are real, visible results. Vague, abstract and theoretical are what the speeches offered.

o: The clinic was the first tangible benefit the village saw from the scheme.
The benefits were tangible, though no one could see, measure or point to any.
His tangible fears were entirely imaginary, as he later admitted himself.
The plan stayed tangible, existing only as an idea in the minister's head.
cards.why: Tangible means real and measurable, so invisible benefits, imaginary fears and a mere idea all contradict it.

words.meaning: Having a strong wish for revenge
words.note: Latin vindicta = vengeance. Not to be confused with vindicate, to clear of blame.

cards.q: Passed over for promotion, the ___ manager spent the next year undermining his new boss.
cards.why: Spending a year getting even is vengeful. Vindicated means cleared of blame, vivacious means lively, victorious means winning.

o: Her vindictive review was clearly revenge for an old rejection.
The vindictive winner warmly shook hands with every one of his rivals.
In a vindictive mood, she forgave everyone and baked them all a cake.
His vindictive nature meant he never held a grudge for more than a minute.
cards.why: Vindictive means seeking revenge, so warm handshakes, forgiveness and no grudges all contradict it.

idioms.idiom: The chickens come home to roost
idioms.meaning: Past mistakes or wrongdoings eventually bring their consequences
idioms.origin: An old English saying: curses, like chickens, always return to where they came from.
idioms.caption: They always find their way back.

cards.q: For years the firm skipped safety checks; when the bridge it built failed an inspection, the chickens came home to roost. This means ___.
o: Its past wrongdoing finally caught up with it
It was blamed unfairly for someone else's work
It ended up profiting from its earlier risks
Its old staff returned to help fix the problem
cards.why: The consequences of earlier wrongs arriving later is the chickens coming home to roost.

cards.q: He had lied on his CV for a decade, and the background check for his dream job finally exposed it. ___.
o: The chickens had come home to roost
He had rested on his laurels
He had poured oil on troubled waters
cards.why: An old misdeed catching up is the chickens coming home to roost. Crying wolf is raising false alarms.

idioms.meaning: To be nowhere near as good as someone or something
idioms.origin: An apprentice once held a candle for a master craftsman to see by; someone who could not even do that was hopelessly inferior.
idioms.caption: Not even good enough to hold the light.

cards.q: The remake is slick, but it can't hold a candle to the original. The remake is ___.
o: Nowhere near as good as the original
Almost exactly the same as the original
Much darker than the original film
Better than the original in most ways
cards.why: The idiom always marks something as far inferior.

cards.q: The new vendor's samosas are fine, but next to the ones from the old shop by the station they taste of nothing. They ___.
o: can't hold a candle to the old shop's
are stealing the old shop's thunder already
are a flash in the pan
cards.why: Being far inferior is not being able to hold a candle to something. Stealing someone's thunder is taking their moment.

words.meaning: Cautious about possible dangers or problems
words.note: Old English waer = aware, careful.

cards.q: After being cheated once, she was ___ of any offer that sounded too good to be true.
cards.why: Being cheated makes one cautious. Fond is affectionate, ignorant is unaware, envious is jealous.

o: The deer stayed wary, lifting its head at every crack of a twig.
Wary of strangers, the child ran straight up to every new face in the park.
He was wary of the deal and signed it at once without reading a word.
Being wary by nature, she trusted everyone she met completely and instantly.
cards.why: Wary means cautious, so running to strangers, signing unread and trusting instantly all contradict it.

words.meaning: To warn or reprimand someone firmly
words.note: Latin admonere = to remind, warn.

cards.q: The judge ___ the lawyer for interrupting the witness a third time.
cards.why: A judge reacting to repeated interruption would reprimand. Commended and congratulated both praise; acquitted clears.

cards.q: A referee calls a player over, wags a finger and warns him that the next foul will earn a card. The referee ___ him.
cards.why: A firm warning is admonishing. Exonerated means cleared, lauded means praised, cajoled means coaxed.

words.meaning: Gentle and kindly; (in medicine) not harmful
words.note: Latin benignus = kind-hearted. Its opposite is malign or malignant.

cards.q: Relief filled the room when the doctor said the lump was ___.
cards.why: Relief follows news that a growth is harmless. Malignant, fatal and contagious would cause alarm.

o: The climate here is benign, with mild winters and gentle summers.
The benign tumour spread quickly and became life-threatening within weeks.
With a benign scowl, he threatened to have the whole team dismissed.
The benign dictator jailed anyone who dared to criticise him in public.
cards.why: Benign means harmless and kindly, so a spreading tumour, a threat and jailing critics all contradict it.

words.meaning: To force someone to do something by threats or pressure
words.note: Latin coercere = to restrain.

cards.q: The confession was thrown out because police had ___ him into signing it.
cards.why: Forcing a signature makes a confession invalid. Coaxed is gentle persuasion, coalesced means merged, coincided means happened together.

o: Workers were coerced into unpaid overtime by threats of dismissal.
She coerced him gently, offering only kind words and a free choice.
He coerced them by leaving the decision entirely up to them.
He coerced the jury by presenting fair, calm and well-documented evidence.
cards.why: Coerce means force by pressure, so gentle free choice, leaving the decision to them and fair evidence all contradict it.

words.meaning: To mock or express contempt for
words.note: Latin deridere = to laugh down, from ridere, to laugh, as in ridicule.

cards.q: Critics ___ the design as 'a shoebox on stilts', but tourists queue for hours to see it.
cards.why: 'A shoebox on stilts' is mockery, set against the queues by 'but'. Praised, funded and copied do not match the insult.

cards.q: When the young scientist first suggested that ulcers were caused by bacteria, senior doctors laughed at him in conferences. They ___ his idea.
cards.why: Laughing at an idea is deriding it. Venerated means revered, corroborated means confirmed, embellished means decorated.

idioms.meaning: To betray someone who trusted you
idioms.origin: From American slavery, when enslaved people were sold 'down the river' to harsher plantations in the Deep South.
idioms.caption: A handshake, then a betrayal.

cards.q: The union leader sold his members down the river by secretly agreeing to the pay cut. He ___.
o: Betrayed the people who trusted him
Negotiated hard but lost in the end
Made an honest mistake in the talks
Left them to fight the battle alone
cards.why: The idiom is about betrayal of trust, not defeat or desertion.

cards.q: She promised to back her partner at the board meeting, then voted to remove him in exchange for his job. She ___.
cards.why: Betraying someone who relied on you is selling them down the river. Throwing down the gauntlet is issuing a challenge.

idioms.meaning: A final performance or achievement before retirement or death
idioms.origin: From the ancient belief that a swan, silent all its life, sings one beautiful song just before it dies.
idioms.caption: Silent all its life. One last song.

cards.q: The veteran's century in his final Test was a fitting swan song. It was ___.
o: A last great performance before retiring
A surprising comeback after a long absence
A lucky innings that hid poor form
His very first appearance for the country
cards.why: A swan song is specifically a final performance.

cards.q: The architect's last building before she retired is now considered her finest work. It was her ___.
cards.why: A final achievement before leaving is a swan song. Waterloo is a final defeat, not a final triumph.

words.meaning: To decorate, or to add untrue details to a story to make it more interesting
words.note: Old French bel = beautiful.

cards.q: Every time he told the fishing story, he ___ it a little more, until the fish was bigger than the boat.
cards.why: Making the fish grow with each telling is adding untrue detail. Summarised shortens, retracted withdraws, fact-checked tests it.

o: She embellished the plain cake with sugared roses and gold leaf.
He embellished the report by cutting it down to the bare facts and figures.
The witness embellished her account by repeating it exactly, word for word.
They embellished the hall by removing every chair, light and curtain.
cards.why: Embellish means add decoration or detail, so cutting down, repeating exactly and stripping a hall all contradict it.

words.meaning: A mistaken belief, or an argument built on faulty reasoning
words.note: Latin fallere = to deceive, as in fallible and false.

cards.q: It is a ___ that you lose most of your body heat through your head.
cards.why: A widely believed but wrong idea is a fallacy. A fact is true, a statistic is a figure, a precaution is a safety step.

cards.q: A gambler who has lost ten times in a row bets everything, sure that he is now 'due' a win. His thinking rests on a ___.
cards.why: Each bet is independent, so the belief he is 'due' is faulty reasoning. A premise is a starting point, certainty is sureness, a precedent is an earlier example.

words.meaning: Uncalled for; done without good reason
words.note: Latin gratuitus = freely given, from gratia, favour.

cards.q: The film was spoiled by ___ violence that added nothing to the story.
cards.why: Violence that adds nothing is uncalled for. Essential and justified mean it was needed, and understated does not fit 'spoiled'.

o: His gratuitous insult about her accent had nothing to do with the debate.
The gratuitous scene was the only part essential to understanding the plot.
She made a gratuitous point that was central to the case and won the trial.
The gratuitous rule was introduced after careful study of a real, serious danger.
cards.why: Gratuitous means without good reason, so being essential, central or carefully justified all contradict it.

words.meaning: Unlucky and unfortunate
words.note: Old Norse happ = luck, as in happen and haphazard; hapless = without luck.

cards.q: The ___ tourist missed the last train, lost his wallet and then got caught in the rain.
cards.why: Three misfortunes in a row make someone unlucky. Fortunate is the opposite, reckless and fearless describe character, not luck.

cards.q: The ___ goalkeeper slipped just as he was about to collect the easy ball.
cards.why: Slipping at the worst moment is bad luck. Heedless means careless, helpless means unable to help oneself, harmless means safe.

words.meaning: Without any fault or flaw
words.note: Latin in- (not) + peccare (to sin): incapable of sinning.

cards.q: Her English was so ___ that the interviewers assumed she had studied abroad.
cards.why: English good enough to suggest study abroad is flawless. Halting, mediocre and unremarkable are all weaker.

o: The hotel's service was impeccable, from the welcome to the farewell.
His impeccable record included three warnings and a suspension.
She has impeccable taste and filled the room with mismatched clutter.
The impeccable report was riddled with errors on almost every page.
cards.why: Impeccable means faultless, so warnings, clutter and errors all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: A person who lives a lazy, dreamy life, forgetful of duties
idioms.origin: In Homer's Odyssey, sailors who ate the lotus fruit lost all wish to return home and wanted only to stay and drift.
idioms.caption: One taste and you forget the way home.

cards.q: After moving to Goa, he became a lotus-eater, forgetting his plans for the novel and the business. He became ___.
o: Someone drifting in lazy pleasure, forgetting duties
A man who works very hard, but only on the things he likes
A traveller who keeps moving from place to place
A dreamer who makes big plans and keeps them all
cards.why: A lotus-eater drifts in comfort and forgets responsibilities.

cards.q: The prince spent his days lounging in the palace gardens, leaving the kingdom's affairs entirely to his ministers. He was ___.
cards.why: Dreamy idleness that forgets duty is the life of a lotus-eater. A Cassandra makes true warnings nobody believes.

idioms.meaning: To issue a challenge
idioms.origin: A medieval knight threw his armoured glove, the gauntlet, to the ground to challenge an opponent to combat.
idioms.caption: Pick it up, and the fight is on.

cards.q: The new start-up threw down the gauntlet by offering free delivery in every city its rival served. It ___.
o: Asked its rival for a partnership
cards.why: Throwing down the gauntlet is an open challenge.

cards.q: The champion announced on live television that she would race anyone, anywhere, for any prize they named. She had ___.
cards.why: Openly inviting anyone to compete is throwing down the gauntlet. Showing the white feather is cowardice.

words.meaning: Sharp and clear in thinking or expression; getting to the heart of a matter
words.note: Latin incidere = to cut into, as in incision.

cards.q: In one ___ question, the interviewer exposed the flaw that the candidate had hidden for twenty minutes.
cards.why: A single question that exposes the key flaw is sharp. Rambling and vague are unfocused, timid is hesitant.

cards.q: Her ___ analysis cut straight through the jargon to the real problem.
cards.why: Cutting straight to the problem is incisive. Indecisive means unable to decide, incessant means non-stop, inclusive means including all.

words.meaning: To express sorrow or regret; an expression of grief
words.note: Latin lamentum = wailing, weeping.

cards.q: Old residents ___ the loss of the banyan tree that had shaded the square for a century.
cards.why: Grieving for a lost landmark is lamenting. Celebrated, ignored and approved do not fit 'the loss'.

o: Teachers lament that students now read so few books for pleasure.
He lamented his promotion by throwing a party for the whole office.
The fans lamented the victory with songs and dancing through the night.
She lamented the good news cheerfully to everyone she met that day.
cards.why: Lament means express sorrow, so a party, celebration and cheerful sharing all contradict it.

words.meaning: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
words.note: Latin meticulosus = fearful, from metus, fear: fearful of making a mistake.

cards.q: The forger was ___, copying even the smudge on the original signature.
cards.why: Copying even a smudge shows extreme care over detail. Happy-go-lucky, hurried and sloppy are the opposite.

cards.q: An editor checks every date against two sources, measures each margin and reads the proofs backwards to catch typos. She is ___.
cards.why: Extreme care over every detail is meticulous. Feckless is irresponsible, impetuous is rash, supercilious is haughty.

words.meaning: So surprised and confused that one does not know how to react
words.note: Latin non plus, no more: brought to a point where nothing more can be said. Often misused to mean unbothered, which is the opposite.

cards.q: The minister was ___ when the schoolgirl asked him to explain his own policy, and stood silent for a full minute.
cards.why: Standing silent, unable to respond, is being nonplussed. Self-possessed and unmoved suggest calm, and delighted suggests pleasure.

o: Nonplussed by the odd question, the candidate stared at the panel.
Completely nonplussed, she answered at once with calm, confident ease.
He was nonplussed and knew exactly what to say and how to say it.
The nonplussed host smoothly handled the surprise without missing a beat.
cards.why: Nonplussed means baffled and at a loss, so calm ease, knowing exactly what to say and smooth handling all contradict it.

words.meaning: To remove a need or difficulty; to make unnecessary
words.note: Latin obviare = to meet in the way, to prevent.

cards.q: The new online form ___ the need to visit the office in person.
cards.why: A form that removes the need for a visit obviates it. Increases, demands and confirms all keep the need.

cards.q: Installing smoke detectors can ___ much of the danger of a night-time fire.
cards.why: Detectors remove a risk before it happens: obviate. Obliterate means destroy, obligate means bind by duty, obfuscate means make unclear.

idioms.meaning: To treat someone's wishes or rights with arrogant disregard
idioms.origin: A roughshod horse had nails projecting from its shoes for grip, and would injure whatever it trampled.
idioms.caption: Spiked shoes. Trampled ground.

cards.q: The developer rode roughshod over the residents' objections and built the tower anyway. He ___.
o: Persuaded them with a better design
cards.why: Riding roughshod is trampling on others' concerns without regard.

cards.q: The new principal scrapped the student council, cancelled the festival and changed the timetable without consulting anyone. She ___ the school community.
o: poured oil on troubled waters for
cards.why: Overriding everyone's wishes without regard is riding roughshod over them. Pouring oil on troubled waters is calming a conflict.

idioms.idiom: Nail one's colours to the mast
idioms.meaning: To declare one's position firmly and refuse to back down
idioms.origin: A warship's flag, its colours, was lowered to surrender; nailing it to the mast meant it could never be lowered.
idioms.caption: This flag is not coming down.

cards.q: Before the vote she nailed her colours to the mast, saying she would resign if the bill passed. She ___.
o: Took a firm public stand she would not abandon
Kept her real views secret until the last moment
Changed her position to match the majority
Refused to take part in the vote at all
cards.why: The idiom is about committing openly and irreversibly to a position.

cards.q: While other columnists hedged, he wrote that the merger would fail and said he would stake his reputation on it. He had ___.
o: nailed his colours to the mast
strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel
cards.why: Declaring a firm position publicly is nailing one's colours to the mast. Showing the white feather is cowardice, the opposite.

words.meaning: So intense or obvious it can almost be touched
words.note: Latin palpare = to touch gently, as in palpitate.

cards.q: The tension in the room was ___ as the results were read out.
cards.why: Tension you can almost feel is palpable. Imperceptible, imaginary and negligible all mean it barely exists.

o: There was a palpable sense of relief when the lost child was found.
Her palpable joy was so faint that no one around her noticed it.
The palpable difference between the two copies was invisible even under a lens.
A palpable silence hung in the hall, broken by constant chatter and laughter.
cards.why: Palpable means obvious enough to feel, so unnoticed joy, an invisible difference and a silence full of chatter all contradict it.

words.meaning: Aggressively greedy, especially for money
words.note: Latin rapere = to seize, as in rapt and rapture.

cards.q: The ___ landlord raised the rent three times in one year and kept every deposit.
cards.why: Repeated rent rises and kept deposits show aggressive greed. Generous and lenient are the opposite; negligent is careless.

cards.q: A moneylender charges 60 per cent interest, seizes farmers' land at the first missed payment and lends again to their sons. He is ___.
cards.why: Grasping, predatory greed is rapacious. Munificent and benevolent are generous and kind; placid is calm.

words.meaning: Very careful to do what is honest and correct; diligent and thorough
words.note: Latin scrupulus = a small sharp stone, a worry that pricks the conscience.

cards.q: The ___ shopkeeper ran after the customer to return the extra fifty rupees.
cards.why: Chasing a customer to return money is honesty. Greedy and cunning would keep it, and absent-minded would not notice.

cards.q: She kept ___ records of every expense, down to the bus tickets.
cards.why: Exact, careful records are scrupulous. Scurrilous means insulting, sumptuous means lavish, spurious means false.

words.meaning: To shorten by cutting off part
words.note: Latin truncare = to maim, from truncus, a tree trunk stripped of branches.

cards.q: The broadcast was ___ when the match ran late, so the last ten minutes of the film were never shown.
cards.why: Losing the last ten minutes means it was cut short. Extended lengthens, repeated shows again, postponed delays.

o: The software truncates long file names after thirty characters.
The editor truncated the essay by adding two new chapters to it.
His truncated speech ran an hour longer than anyone had expected.
They truncated the season by adding three extra matches at the end.
cards.why: Truncate means cut short, so adding chapters, running longer and adding matches all contradict it.

words.meaning: Loud and forceful in expressing opinions
words.note: Latin vox (voice) + ferre (to carry).

cards.q: The plan faced ___ opposition, with residents shouting down every speaker at the meeting.
cards.why: Shouting down speakers is loud, forceful opposition. Muted, tacit and half-hearted are all quiet or weak.

o: She was a vociferous critic of the plan and wrote to every paper.
His vociferous protest was a polite note, quietly slipped under the door.
The vociferous crowd watched the speech in complete, respectful silence.
A vociferous opponent, he never once shared his opinion with anyone.
cards.why: Vociferous means loudly outspoken, so a quiet note, silence and never speaking all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: A person hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts
idioms.origin: The Philistines were biblical enemies of the Israelites; in the 1800s German students used the name for uncultured townspeople.
idioms.caption: A masterpiece? Looks like a mess to me.

cards.q: Only a Philistine would turn the old library into a parking lot, the poet wrote. He meant ___.
o: Someone with no regard for culture
Someone with a strong sense of history
Someone who cannot afford to read books
cards.why: A Philistine is indifferent or hostile to culture, not poor or foreign.

cards.q: Shown a celebrated painting, he asked why anyone would pay crores for 'some splashes of paint' and suggested selling it to fund a car park. He was being ___.
cards.why: Contempt for art is the mark of a Philistine. A lotus-eater drifts in lazy pleasure.

idioms.meaning: To act in a cowardly way
idioms.origin: In cockfighting, a white feather in a bird's tail was thought to mark poor breeding and a lack of fight.
idioms.caption: When it counted, he ran.

cards.q: When asked to testify against his boss, the witness showed the white feather and withdrew his statement. He ___.
o: Told the court the whole truth
Changed his mind after new evidence
Was forced out by the defence lawyers
cards.why: The idiom always means cowardice.

cards.q: He boasted all week about confronting the bully, then pretended to be ill on the day. He ___.
o: nailed his colours to the mast
cards.why: Backing out from fear is showing the white feather. The other three all show courage or commitment.

words.meaning: To decrease gradually in size, strength or importance
words.note: Old English wanian = to lessen; the moon waxes and wanes.

cards.q: Interest in the craze began to ___ after a few months, and the shops cleared their stock at half price.
cards.why: Clearance sales follow fading interest. Surge, peak and spread all describe growth.

o: His influence waned after he lost the party's leadership.
Her popularity waned as millions more fans joined every single month.
The waning moon grew larger and brighter each night of the week.
Support for the plan waned until it was stronger than it had ever been.
cards.why: Wane means decrease, so millions joining, a growing moon and stronger support all contradict it.

words.meaning: To regard with disgust and hatred
words.note: Latin abhorrere = to shrink back in horror.

cards.q: She ___ cruelty to animals and refused to attend the circus.
cards.why: Refusing to attend shows strong disgust. Admired is the opposite, tolerated and overlooked are far too mild.

cards.q: A judge walks out of a dinner the moment a guest tells a joke mocking the poor, and never speaks to him again. She ___ such humour.
cards.why: Walking out and cutting contact show disgust. Relishes means enjoys, condones means accepts, overlooks means ignores.

words.meaning: Showing great care and steady, persistent effort
words.note: Latin assidere = to sit by, to stay at a task.

cards.q: Through ___ practice, two hours every morning for five years, she became the state's top chess player.
cards.why: Two hours daily for five years is steady effort. Sporadic is irregular, casual is relaxed, reluctant is unwilling.

o: An assiduous student, he revised every chapter twice.
Her assiduous effort lasted only until the first difficult problem.
The assiduous clerk left every task half-done and went home early.
With assiduous neglect, the gardener let the roses die of thirst.
cards.why: Assiduous means careful and persistent, so quitting early, half-done tasks and neglect all contradict it.

words.meaning: Mercy, especially in giving a lighter punishment
words.note: Latin clemens = mild, merciful.

cards.q: Given his age and illness, the court showed ___ and suspended the sentence.
cards.why: Suspending a sentence out of compassion is mercy. Severity is harshness, contempt is scorn, haste is speed.

cards.q: The president rejected the plea for ___, and the sentence stood.
cards.why: A plea for a lighter sentence is a plea for clemency. Complacency is smugness, credulity is being too ready to believe, clarity is clearness.

words.meaning: Deceitfulness; saying one thing while doing another
words.note: Latin duplex = double, twofold.

cards.q: A politician promises farmers higher prices and, in the same week, quietly signs a deal that lowers them. His conduct shows ___.
cards.why: Saying one thing and doing the opposite is double-dealing. Probity and forthrightness mean honesty, clemency means mercy.

o: Her duplicity came out when the rivals compared her promises.
His duplicity was clear from how plainly and honestly he spoke to everyone.
The duplicity of the deal was that every term was open and fair to both sides.
With complete duplicity, she told everyone the same truth in the same words.
cards.why: Duplicity is double-dealing, so plain honesty, fair open terms and telling everyone the same truth all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: Simple, austere and without comfort or luxury
idioms.origin: Ancient Sparta trained its citizens in hardship from childhood, with plain food and harsh discipline.
idioms.caption: One bed. One bowl. Nothing else.

cards.q: The hostel room was Spartan: a cot, a bucket and a nail to hang a shirt on. It was ___.
o: Plain and bare, with no comforts
Crowded and noisy all night long
cards.why: Spartan means simple and austere, not dirty, crowded or overpriced.

cards.q: The monk's cell held nothing but a mat and a lamp, and he ate a single bowl of rice a day. His life was ___.
cards.why: Austere simplicity is Spartan. Draconian is excessive harshness in punishment.

idioms.meaning: To end a quarrel and make peace
idioms.origin: Some Native American nations marked peace by literally burying a war axe, a hatchet, in the ground.
idioms.caption: Put the weapon in the ground.

cards.q: After ten years of not speaking, the two brothers buried the hatchet at their mother's birthday. They ___.
o: Ended their quarrel and made peace
Agreed to divide the family property
Promised never to meet each other again
Kept the reason for the quarrel secret
cards.why: Burying the hatchet is ending a feud.

cards.q: The rival captains, who had refused to shake hands for years, finally shared a joke and posed together for the cameras. They had ___.
o: sold each other down the river
cards.why: Making peace after a long feud is burying the hatchet. Throwing down the gauntlet starts a fight instead.

words.meaning: Unreasonably high, especially of a price
words.note: Latin ex (out of) + orbita (track): going off the track.

cards.q: The airport café charged an ___ four hundred rupees for a cup of tea.
cards.why: Four hundred rupees for tea is unreasonably high. Modest, reasonable and nominal all mean low or fair.

o: Families complained about the exorbitant fees the private school charged.
The exorbitant price was so low that students could easily afford it.
She bought the shirt at an exorbitant discount of nearly ninety per cent.
Rents became exorbitant when they dropped to half their previous level.
cards.why: Exorbitant means unreasonably high, so a low price, a huge discount and halved rents all contradict it.

words.meaning: Innocent and unsuspecting; trusting to the point of naivety
words.note: Latin ingenuus = freeborn, frank. Not to be confused with ingenious, which means clever.

cards.q: It was ___ of her to believe the stranger who said he was a bank officer.
cards.why: Trusting a stranger is naive. Ingenious means clever, disingenuous means pretending to be innocent, ingenuity is a noun meaning cleverness.

cards.q: A first-year student lends his bike, his notes and his phone to anyone who asks, and is surprised every time something is not returned. He is ___.
cards.why: Innocent trust that keeps being surprised is ingenuous. Cynical and wary expect the worst, duplicitous is deceitful.

words.meaning: An outcast; a person rejected by society
words.note: From Tamil paraiyar, the name of a community of drummers once excluded by the caste system.

cards.q: After the scandal, the once-popular actor became a ___ that no studio would hire.
cards.why: No studio hiring him means he is an outcast. Celebrity, mentor and icon all suggest esteem.

o: Its nuclear tests made the country a global pariah for a decade.
As the town's pariah, he was invited to every wedding and festival.
The pariah of the class was the student everyone wanted to sit with.
She became a pariah when the whole industry rushed to work with her.
cards.why: A pariah is shunned, so being invited everywhere, sought after and in demand all contradict it.

words.meaning: To think deeply and at length about something
words.note: Latin ruminari = to chew the cud, as cows do: going over the same thing again and again.

cards.q: He spent the whole train journey ___ on what the interviewer had meant by 'interesting'.
cards.why: Spending a journey turning over one word is deep, repeated thought. Dozing, gossiping and bargaining do not fit.

cards.q: She sat on the porch to ___ over the offer before giving her answer.
cards.why: Thinking an offer over is ruminating. Rejuvenate means make young again, remunerate means pay, ruin means destroy.

words.meaning: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, often for the worse
words.note: Latin volare = to fly; volatile substances evaporate, flying off as vapour.

cards.q: With prices swinging ten per cent in a day, the market was too ___ for first-time investors.
cards.why: Ten per cent daily swings mean an unstable market. Stable and predictable are the opposite, sluggish means slow-moving.

o: The border was volatile, and talks could collapse at any moment.
His volatile temper stayed perfectly steady through every crisis he faced.
The volatile prices had not moved a single rupee in over ten years.
She has a volatile nature and has never once changed her mood or mind.
cards.why: Volatile means liable to sudden change, so steady temper, unmoved prices and a never-changing mood all contradict it.

idioms.idiom: Strain at a gnat and swallow a camel
idioms.meaning: To fuss over trivial matters while ignoring serious ones
idioms.origin: From the Gospel of Matthew, criticising those who filter a tiny gnat out of their drink but gulp down a whole camel.
idioms.caption: Caught the gnat. Missed the camel.

cards.q: The auditors queried a fifty-rupee taxi bill but missed the crore that had vanished. They strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel, meaning they ___.
o: Fussed over trifles, missed the real problem
Were careful with every expense, large or small
Exaggerated a small error into a scandal
Were bribed to overlook the missing money
cards.why: The idiom pairs fussing over small things with ignoring the big ones.

cards.q: The school banned coloured socks for being 'disruptive' while ignoring reports of serious bullying in the hostel. It was ___.
o: straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel
killing the goose that lays the golden eggs
cards.why: Fussing over trifles while ignoring a grave matter is straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. Penny wise, pound foolish is about money specifically.

idioms.meaning: A question open to debate, or one no longer worth discussing
idioms.origin: A moot was an Anglo-Saxon assembly where questions were debated; law students still argue hypothetical 'moot' cases.
idioms.caption: Debate it all you like. It changes nothing.

cards.q: Whether the bus or the train is faster became a moot point once the roads were closed. It became ___.
o: A question no longer worth arguing
The most important question to settle
A question everyone finally agreed on
A question only experts could answer
cards.why: A moot point is debatable or no longer relevant; here, the closure made the question pointless.

cards.q: They argued for an hour about who would host the party, only to learn it had been cancelled. The argument was now ___.
cards.why: A question made irrelevant by events is a moot point. A red herring is a deliberate distraction.

words.meaning: Bitterness and ill feeling, especially in speech or argument
words.note: Latin acer = sharp, sour, as in acid and acrid.

cards.q: The meeting ended in ___, with both founders shouting and one storming out.
cards.why: Shouting and storming out show bitter ill feeling. Harmony and consensus mean agreement; laughter does not fit.

o: The divorce was settled without acrimony; they still share a Diwali meal.
Their acrimony showed in the warm, generous toast he made at her farewell.
With great acrimony, the rivals hugged and thanked each other for the match.
The acrimony between the teams was so slight that they shared a single bus.
cards.why: Acrimony is bitterness, so a warm toast, hugs and happily sharing a bus all contradict it.

words.meaning: To make pain, a problem or suffering less severe
words.note: Latin levis = light, as in levity and elevate: to lighten.

cards.q: The new flyover was meant to ___ traffic, but it simply moved the jam two kilometres away.
cards.why: A flyover is meant to ease traffic; the 'but' shows it failed. Aggravate means worsen, create and celebrate do not fit.

cards.q: A cold compress can ___ the swelling after a sprain.
cards.why: Reducing swelling is alleviating it. Alienate means estrange, allocate means distribute, alliterate means repeat starting sounds.

words.meaning: A deep-seated feeling of dislike
words.note: Greek anti (against) + pathos (feeling). Compare sympathy and apathy.

cards.q: A writer refuses every invitation from the city's literary festival, mocks it in every column and crosses the road to avoid its director. He feels ___ towards it.
cards.why: Active, deep dislike is antipathy. Apathy and indifference mean not caring at all, sympathy is fellow feeling.

o: Her antipathy to cricket was so strong that she left the room when it came on.
His antipathy for the city made him move there and stay for forty happy years.
Out of sheer antipathy, she named her daughter after her favourite aunt.
Their antipathy showed in how often and eagerly they chose to meet up.
cards.why: Antipathy is deep dislike, so moving there happily, honouring someone and eager meetings all contradict it.

words.meaning: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason
words.note: Latin arbiter = a judge; an arbitrary decision rests on one person's will alone.

cards.q: The cut-off of 87.5 per cent seemed ___; no one could explain why it was not 85 or 90.
cards.why: A number nobody can justify is arbitrary. Logical and scientific imply reasons; generous does not fit.

o: Workers objected to the arbitrary rule that changed with the manager's mood.
The arbitrary schedule was carefully built around every team member's needs.
Her arbitrary choice was based on three months of detailed research.
The judge's arbitrary ruling followed the law exactly, line by line.
cards.why: Arbitrary means without reason, so careful planning, research and following the law exactly all contradict it.

words.meaning: Involving great effort; difficult and tiring
words.note: Latin arduus = steep, high.

cards.q: After an ___ climb of nine hours, the trekkers reached the pass at sunset.
cards.why: Nine hours of climbing is hard work. Effortless, leisurely and brief all describe the opposite.

cards.q: A student revises for two years, wakes at five, sits forty mocks and gives up every holiday to clear the exam. Her preparation was ___.
cards.why: Two years of exhausting effort is arduous. Perfunctory, desultory and cursory all describe careless or half-hearted effort.

idioms.meaning: A task requiring enormous strength or effort
idioms.origin: Hercules, hero of Greek myth, had to complete twelve near-impossible labours, such as killing the many-headed Hydra.
idioms.caption: Twelve labours. Every one impossible.

cards.q: Cleaning up the river after decades of factory waste is a Herculean task. It is ___.
o: A job that can never succeed
A job best left to experts
cards.why: Herculean means enormously demanding, but possible. A task that can never succeed would be Sisyphean.

cards.q: Digitising a hundred years of handwritten court records with a team of three is ___.
cards.why: A job of enormous scale is a Herculean task. A busman's holiday is a break spent doing your usual work.

idioms.meaning: To make an offer of peace or reconciliation
idioms.origin: In the story of Noah, a dove returns with an olive leaf, a sign the flood is over; in Greece and Rome the olive branch stood for peace.
idioms.caption: An offer, not a surrender.

cards.q: After the bitter strike, the management held out an olive branch by inviting the union to dinner. It ___.
cards.why: An olive branch is a peace gesture, not an admission or a concession.

cards.q: Months after their quarrel, he sent his old friend a birthday card and asked if they could meet for coffee. He was ___.
o: pulling the wool over his eyes
cards.why: Offering to make peace is holding out an olive branch. Throwing down the gauntlet is the opposite: a challenge.

words.meaning: Quick to see and turn a situation to one's advantage; shrewd
words.note: Latin astus = craft, cunning.

cards.q: An ___ investor, she sold her shares a week before the crash.
cards.why: Selling just before a crash shows shrewd judgement. Naive, reckless and indolent would have missed it.

o: His astute reading of the market made the small shop the town's biggest.
The astute buyer paid twice the price for a fake without asking a question.
She was astute enough to sign the contract without reading a single line.
An astute general, he marched his army straight into an obvious trap.
