cards.why: Astute means shrewd, so paying for a fake, signing unread and walking into a trap all contradict it.

words.meaning: To give a false impression of; to contradict
words.note: Old English beleogan = to deceive by lying.

cards.q: His calm voice ___ the panic he felt as the plane lost height.
cards.why: A calm voice giving a false picture of inner panic belies it. Revealed and matched would show it honestly; increased does not fit.

cards.q: The old car looks rusty and battered, yet it has won the hill climb three years running. Its appearance ___ its performance.
cards.why: When looks give a false idea of reality, they belie it. Reflects, confirms and predicts all mean the look matches the truth.

words.meaning: High-sounding but with little meaning; pompous
words.note: Bombast was cotton padding for clothes, so bombastic speech is padded and puffed up.

cards.q: The minister's ___ speech promised 'a new dawn for humanity' but contained no actual plan.
cards.why: Grand words with no substance are bombastic. Understated, modest and laconic all mean restrained.

cards.q: Stripped of its ___ language, the report said only that sales had fallen.
cards.why: Puffed-up wording hiding a simple point is bombastic. Ballistic relates to projectiles, bureaucratic to officials, bucolic to the countryside.

words.meaning: Bold and without shame
words.note: Old English braesen = made of brass, hard and shameless.

cards.q: In a ___ theft, the gang drove a truck into the showroom in broad daylight.
cards.why: A daylight truck raid is shamelessly bold. Furtive and discreet mean secretive, timid means shy.

o: He told a brazen lie to the judge, though the video proved otherwise.
The brazen thief crept in at night and was careful to leave no trace.
With brazen modesty, she hid her prize and refused to mention it.
His brazen apology was full of shame and quiet regret for his acts.
cards.why: Brazen means shamelessly bold, so creeping secretly, modesty and shame all contradict it.

words.meaning: To grow or increase rapidly; to flourish
words.note: Old French burjon = a bud, a shoot.

cards.q: With the new metro line, cafés and coaching centres began to ___ around every station.
cards.why: Businesses springing up quickly is burgeoning. Dwindle and vanish mean shrink, stagnate means stand still.

cards.q: A town of 20,000 grows to 200,000 in ten years after a tech park opens. Its population has ___.
cards.why: Rapid growth is burgeoning. Plummeted means fell sharply, stabilised means levelled off, waned means declined.

idioms.meaning: A difficult first experience of something
idioms.origin: Originally a soldier's first experience of battle; earlier, a spiritual baptism through suffering.
idioms.caption: First day. Worst day.

cards.q: Her first week as a nurse coincided with the floods, a real baptism of fire. It was ___.
o: A lucky start to her career
cards.why: A baptism of fire is a tough introduction to something new.

cards.q: The new captain's first match was a final against the world champions, in front of eighty thousand people. It was ___.
o: the straw that broke the camel's back
cards.why: A brutally hard first experience is a baptism of fire. A swan song is a last performance, not a first.

idioms.meaning: To be good enough; to reach the required standard
idioms.origin: American slang from around 1900, where 'the mustard' meant the best of something.
idioms.caption: Good enough? Just about.

cards.q: The trial batsman was fast and fearless but simply didn't cut the mustard against spin. He ___.
cards.why: Not cutting the mustard means failing to meet the standard.

cards.q: Of the forty applicants for the chef's post, only two produced dishes that were good enough for the restaurant. Only two ___.
cards.why: Meeting the standard is cutting the mustard. Meeting one's Waterloo is a final defeat.

words.meaning: Bad-tempered, argumentative and uncooperative
words.note: Possibly from Middle English contack, a quarrel.

cards.q: The ___ old neighbour complained about the children's noise, the dog, and even the birds.
cards.why: Complaining about everything shows a bad temper. Good-humoured, placid and benevolent are all good-natured.

o: A cantankerous passenger argued with every crew member on the flight.
The cantankerous host welcomed each guest with warm smiles and sweets.
She grew cantankerous with age and agreed cheerfully to every request.
His cantankerous nature made him the calmest peacemaker in the office.
cards.why: Cantankerous means argumentative and grumpy, so warm welcomes, cheerful agreement and peacemaking all contradict it.

words.meaning: To express strong official disapproval; such disapproval
words.note: Latin censura, the office of the Roman censor, who judged citizens' conduct.

cards.q: The council voted to ___ the member who had leaked confidential papers.
cards.why: Officially condemning someone is censuring them. Censor means cut content, censorship is that cutting, a sensor detects things.

cards.q: Parliament passes a formal motion declaring that a minister misled the house and must apologise. The motion ___ him.
cards.why: A formal statement of disapproval censures. Exonerates clears, venerates reveres, commends praises.

words.meaning: The use of trickery to achieve a purpose
words.note: French chicaner = to quibble, to play tricks in law.

cards.q: The deal was won through legal ___: hidden clauses, false deadlines and a forged signature.
cards.why: Hidden clauses and forgery are trickery. Integrity, transparency and diligence are honest virtues.

o: Voters grew tired of the chicanery that marked every local election.
His chicanery was admired for being open, honest and fully above board.
Through careful chicanery, she made sure every term was fair to both sides.
The chicanery of the audit was its plain, accurate and honest reporting.
cards.why: Chicanery is trickery, so openness, fairness and honest reporting all contradict it.

words.meaning: Corresponding in size or degree; in proportion
words.note: Latin com- (together) + mensurare (to measure).

cards.q: The salary will be ___ with experience: the more years you bring, the more you earn.
cards.why: Pay that rises with experience is in proportion to it. Unrelated and indifferent deny any link, and disproportionate means out of proportion.

cards.q: A boy who broke one window is fined ten thousand rupees and suspended for a term. Critics say the punishment is not ___ with the offence.
cards.why: A punishment out of proportion is not commensurate. Coincident means happening together, concurrent means at the same time, contemporaneous means of the same period.

words.meaning: Intended to calm anger and restore goodwill
words.note: Latin conciliare = to bring together, to win over.

cards.q: After the angry exchange, the manager struck a ___ tone and offered to review the decision.
cards.why: Offering a review after anger is calming. Belligerent, defiant and confrontational are all hostile.

o: As a conciliatory gesture, she asked her rival to co-chair the panel.
His conciliatory remarks only enraged the crowd further, as he intended.
The conciliatory letter threatened legal action within twenty-four hours.
With a conciliatory sneer, he dismissed the complaint as pure nonsense.
cards.why: Conciliatory means seeking to calm, so enraging on purpose, threats and a dismissive sneer all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: To accept the authority or rules of a group
idioms.origin: Runners and sailors once had to place their toes exactly on a line before starting or for inspection.
idioms.caption: Feet on the line. No arguments.

cards.q: Ministers who disagreed in private still toed the line in parliament. They ___.
o: Resigned rather than vote for the bill
Abstained when it came to the vote
cards.why: Toeing the line is conforming to the group's position, whatever one thinks privately.

cards.q: New recruits who questioned the rules were warned that they would have to obey them or leave. They had to ___.
cards.why: Conforming to authority is toeing the line. Cutting the Gordian knot is solving a knotty problem boldly.

idioms.meaning: To be in a very precarious state
idioms.origin: Echoes the sword of Damocles, hanging over a man's head by a single hair.
idioms.caption: One snip, and it's all over.

cards.q: After the third failed rescue plan, the airline's future was hanging by a thread. It was ___.
o: Being sold off to a rival
cards.why: Hanging by a thread means close to failing, with little holding it up.

cards.q: The patient's life depended on whether the one available donor organ arrived in time. His life was ___.
cards.why: A situation that could collapse at any moment is hanging by a thread. A curate's egg is something partly good, partly bad.

words.meaning: Abundant in supply or quantity
words.note: Latin copia = plenty, as in cornucopia.

cards.q: She took ___ notes, filling three notebooks in a single lecture series.
cards.why: Three notebooks is a great quantity. Sparse, meagre and insufficient all mean small amounts.

o: The guests were served copious amounts of food at the wedding.
There was copious water, barely a cupful for the whole village.
He shed copious tears, so few that nobody saw him crying at all.
The copious evidence fit on one small slip of paper, half-empty.
cards.why: Copious means plentiful, so a cupful, unseen tears and a half-empty slip all contradict it.

words.meaning: To confirm or support a statement or theory with evidence
words.note: Latin corroborare = to strengthen, from robur, strength.

cards.q: Two witnesses ___ her account, and the CCTV footage settled the matter.
cards.why: Witnesses supporting an account corroborate it. Contradicted opposes, invented fabricates, ignored disregards.

cards.q: Without evidence to ___ his claim, the court refused to act on it.
cards.why: Evidence confirming a claim corroborates it. Collaborate means work together, corrode means wear away, correlate means relate.

words.meaning: Hasty and therefore not thorough
words.note: Latin cursor = a runner.

cards.q: A ___ glance at the report missed the error that a careful reading would have caught.
cards.why: A glance that misses errors is hasty. Meticulous, exhaustive and rigorous all describe careful reading.

cards.q: An inspector walks through a twelve-storey building in ten minutes, ticks every box and certifies it safe. His inspection was ___.
cards.why: Ten minutes for twelve storeys is hasty and superficial. Assiduous, scrupulous and painstaking all mean thorough.

words.meaning: A scarcity or lack of something
words.note: Middle English derthe = costliness, from dear: what is scarce is dear.

cards.q: The college closed its physics department because of a ___ of qualified teachers.
cards.why: Closing for want of teachers means a shortage. Surplus, glut and wealth all mean too many.

o: A dearth of rain this year has left the reservoirs nearly empty.
There was a dearth of volunteers, so many that some were sent home.
The dearth of options left her spoilt for choice among fifty offers.
A dearth of talent meant the team had too many stars to fit in.
cards.why: Dearth means shortage, so excess volunteers, fifty offers and too many stars all contradict it.

words.meaning: A sudden and complete failure; a fiasco
words.note: French débâcle = the breaking up of ice on a river, sweeping everything away.

cards.q: The launch was a ___: the app crashed, the stage lights failed and the CEO forgot his lines.
cards.why: Everything going wrong at once is a fiasco. Triumph, milestone and success are all positive.

cards.q: A team leading 3-0 at half-time concedes five goals in the second half and is knocked out. The match was a ___.
cards.why: A sudden total collapse is a debacle. A stalemate is a deadlock, a landslide is a huge win, a reprieve is a rescue.

idioms.meaning: Completely; including everything
idioms.origin: The three main parts of an old gun: the firing lock, the wooden stock and the barrel.
idioms.caption: Every part. Nothing left behind.

cards.q: When the firm moved to Pune, it shifted lock, stock and barrel. It moved ___.
cards.why: Lock, stock and barrel means wholly, with nothing left out.

cards.q: The collector bought the entire library, every book, shelf and catalogue card. He bought it ___.
o: by the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: Taking absolutely everything is lock, stock and barrel. Penny wise, pound foolish is a false economy.

idioms.meaning: An irreversible decision has been made
idioms.origin: Words attributed to Julius Caesar as he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC: once a dice is thrown, it cannot be taken back.
idioms.caption: Thrown. No taking it back.

cards.q: Once the resignation letter was sent, the die was cast. This means ___.
o: There was no turning back now
It was down to pure luck now
He could still change his mind
cards.why: The die is cast means a step has been taken that cannot be undone.

cards.q: The ballots had been counted and the result announced; whatever came next, the decision could not be reversed. ___.
o: The chickens came home to roost
cards.why: An irreversible decision is the die being cast. The chickens coming home to roost is about consequences of past wrongs.

words.meaning: Behaviour that is proper, polite and dignified
words.note: Latin decorus = seemly, fitting, as in decorate and decent.

cards.q: The judge reminded the shouting lawyers to maintain ___ in her courtroom.
cards.why: A judge asks for dignified behaviour. Chaos is what she is stopping; rivalry and intensity do not fit 'maintain'.

o: Even at the heated debate, both candidates kept their decorum throughout.
With great decorum, he threw his shoe at the speaker and stormed out.
The wedding guests showed decorum by brawling over the last of the sweets.
Her decorum was such that she shouted insults at every waiter in sight.
cards.why: Decorum is dignified behaviour, so throwing shoes, brawling and shouting insults all contradict it.

words.meaning: Causing harm or damage
words.note: Greek deleterios = destructive.

cards.q: Late nights had a ___ effect on his marks, which fell every month.
cards.why: Marks falling every month shows harm. Beneficial and salutary mean helpful; inconsequential means too small to matter.

cards.q: Doctors find that sitting for ten hours a day raises the risk of heart disease, back pain and diabetes. Long sitting is ___ to health.
cards.why: Something that raises disease risk is harmful. Conducive means helpful, incidental means minor, indispensable means essential.

words.meaning: Reserved, modest and shy
words.note: Probably from Old French meur = mature, grave.

cards.q: The ___ girl at the back of the class surprised everyone by winning the debate.
cards.why: The surprise depends on her being quiet and shy. Brash, boisterous and flamboyant are all loud.

cards.q: She gave a ___ smile and looked down at her hands.
cards.why: A modest, shy smile is demure. Demur means to object, demeaning means degrading, demented means mad.

words.meaning: A ruler with absolute power, usually used cruelly
words.note: Greek despotes = master, lord.

cards.q: The ___ jailed every journalist and renamed the capital after himself.
cards.why: Jailing journalists and self-glorification mark a tyrant. A democrat, diplomat or reformer would not do this.

o: The despot ruled by fear, and no one dared speak against him.
The despot shared power equally with an elected, independent parliament.
As a despot, he held free elections and accepted the result when he lost.
The gentle despot asked the people's permission before every decision.
cards.why: A despot holds absolute power, so shared power, free elections and asking permission all contradict it.

words.meaning: A person who dabbles in a subject without real commitment or knowledge
words.note: Italian dilettare = to delight; once a lover of the arts, now a mere dabbler.

cards.q: He has taken up painting, the sitar, astronomy and pottery in two years, giving each up after a few weeks. He is a ___.
cards.why: Dabbling in many things without commitment is the mark of a dilettante. A virtuoso, connoisseur and specialist all have deep skill or knowledge.

cards.q: Critics dismissed the billionaire as a ___ who bought a film studio without ever having watched films seriously.
cards.why: A shallow, uncommitted dabbler is a dilettante. Visionary, pioneer and connoisseur are all compliments.

idioms.meaning: Something that has both good and bad consequences
idioms.origin: A blade sharpened on both sides can cut the enemy, or the person swinging it.
idioms.caption: Cuts both ways.

cards.q: Fame is a double-edged sword: it brings money but destroys privacy. Fame ___.
o: Is useful only to the strong
Is gained and lost very quickly
cards.why: A double-edged sword helps and harms at the same time.

cards.q: Social media lets a small business reach millions, but one bad review can now reach them just as fast. It is ___.
cards.why: Something with both benefits and risks is a double-edged sword. A Trojan horse is a hidden threat in a gift.

idioms.meaning: To reverse a situation and gain the upper hand
idioms.origin: From backgammon, once called 'tables', where reversing the board swapped the players' positions.
idioms.caption: Losing. Then, suddenly, winning.

cards.q: Down two sets, the young player turned the tables and won the next three. She ___.
o: Lost her temper with the umpire
cards.why: Turning the tables is reversing who has the upper hand.

cards.q: The interviewer tried to trap the minister, but the minister produced a document that exposed the channel's own funding. He ___.
cards.why: Reversing the attack onto the attacker is turning the tables. Toeing the line is conforming.

words.meaning: To perceive or recognise something, often with difficulty
words.note: Latin discernere = to separate, distinguish.

cards.q: In the fog, it was hard to ___ the shape of the boat until it was almost at the jetty.
cards.why: Making out a shape in fog is discerning it. Discard means throw away, disturb means interrupt, disguise means conceal.

o: Experts could discern no difference between copy and original.
She discerned the answer by refusing to look at any of the evidence.
He could discern every word clearly, though he heard nothing at all.
The judge discerned the truth by ignoring both of the witnesses.
cards.why: To discern is to perceive, so refusing to look, hearing nothing and ignoring witnesses all contradict it.

words.meaning: The feeling that someone or something is unworthy of respect; to scorn
words.note: Latin dis- (not) + dignare (to deem worthy).

cards.q: The chef looked at the instant noodles with open ___.
cards.why: A chef viewing instant noodles as beneath him shows scorn. Admiration and envy are the opposite; curiosity is neutral.

cards.q: A famous author refuses to read reviews, calls critics 'failed writers' and never replies to them. He treats critics with ___.
cards.why: Treating critics as unworthy is disdain. Deference is respect, clemency is mercy, rapport is a good relationship.

words.meaning: To hide one's true feelings or motives
words.note: Latin dissimulare = to disguise.

cards.q: When asked about the missing funds, he tried to ___, smiling as though nothing were wrong.
cards.why: Hiding guilt behind a smile is dissembling. Disassemble means take apart, dissent means disagree, dismember means cut limbs off.

cards.q: An honest witness has no need to ___; she simply says what she saw.
cards.why: The contrast with honesty points to concealing the truth. Testify, remember and acknowledge are what an honest witness does.

words.meaning: Temporarily inactive, as if asleep
words.note: French dormir = to sleep, as in dormitory.

cards.q: The volcano had been ___ for three hundred years before it erupted.
cards.why: Silent for three centuries before erupting means inactive. Active, volatile and erupting all describe activity.

o: The virus can lie dormant in the body for years.
The dormant account was used every day for purchases large and small.
Her dormant talent was on show at every concert she gave that year.
The seeds stayed dormant, sprouting the very hour they were sown.
cards.why: Dormant means inactive, so daily use, constant concerts and instant sprouting all contradict it.

words.meaning: Insolent or impertinent behaviour; shameless boldness
words.note: Latin effrons = shameless, literally 'without a forehead' that could blush.

cards.q: After crashing my car, he had the ___ to ask me to pay for his scratched phone.
cards.why: Asking the victim to pay is shameless nerve. Humility, decency and self-restraint are the very things he lacked.

cards.q: A student caught copying in an exam complains to the principal that the invigilator disturbed his concentration. He shows remarkable ___.
cards.why: Complaining when caught cheating is shameless boldness. Contrition is remorse, decorum is proper behaviour, diffidence is shyness.

idioms.meaning: A subject of continuing disagreement
idioms.origin: Two dogs fighting over one bone, a picture used since the 1500s.
idioms.caption: One bone. Two dogs.

cards.q: The river's water has been a bone of contention between the two states for decades. It is ___.
cards.why: A bone of contention is what parties keep fighting over.

cards.q: The family has argued about who gets the ancestral house for twenty years, at every wedding and funeral. The house is ___.
cards.why: The subject of an endless quarrel is a bone of contention. A white elephant is costly and useless.

idioms.meaning: To express support for something without acting on it
idioms.origin: Echoes the Bible's complaint about those who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far away.
idioms.caption: All words. No action.

cards.q: The company pays lip service to diversity but has not hired a woman manager in ten years. It ___.
o: Has made it a top priority
Is unsure what the word means
cards.why: Lip service is support in words only.

cards.q: Every party's manifesto praises clean air, yet none has acted on the city's pollution in a decade. They ___ clean air.
cards.why: Praising without acting is paying lip service. Riding roughshod over something is trampling it openly.

words.meaning: Difficult to find, catch or achieve
words.note: Latin eludere = to escape by tricks.

cards.q: After six finals, the trophy remained ___ for the team.
cards.why: Six finals without winning means the trophy kept escaping them. Certain, guaranteed and inevitable mean it was assured.

cards.q: Success proved ___; every time she came close, something went wrong.
cards.why: Something hard to grasp is elusive. Illusive means deceptive, allusive means hinting, exclusive means restricted.

words.meaning: To match or surpass someone, typically by imitation
words.note: Latin aemulus = rival.

cards.q: Young players try to ___ their heroes, copying even the way they celebrate.
cards.why: Copying heroes to match them is emulating. Ridicule, ignore and avoid all mean the opposite.

o: Other states hope to emulate Kerala's success in public health.
He emulated his father by doing the exact opposite of everything he did.
The new school emulated the old one by rejecting all of its methods.
She emulated her coach by refusing to learn anything from her.
cards.why: Emulate means imitate in order to match, so doing the opposite, rejecting methods and refusing to learn all contradict it.

words.meaning: A person or thing that is mysterious or hard to understand
words.note: Greek ainigma = a riddle.

cards.q: The quiet genius remained an ___ to his colleagues, who never knew what he thought.
cards.why: Someone whose thoughts nobody knows is a mystery. An open book is the opposite; inspiration and nuisance do not fit.

cards.q: Nobody knows who built the stone circle, how the stones were moved or what it was for. The monument is an ___.
cards.why: Something deeply mysterious is an enigma. An eyesore is ugly, an anachronism is out of its time, an heirloom is handed down.

words.meaning: Deep hostility between people or groups
words.note: Old French enemistie, from enemi, enemy.

cards.q: The ___ between the two clans went back three generations, to a quarrel over a well.
cards.why: A three-generation feud is deep hostility. Alliance, friendship and kinship are bonds.

o: Years of enmity ended when the rivals finally shook hands on stage.
Their enmity was so warm that they holidayed together every summer.
Out of deep enmity, she gave him her vote and her full support.
The enmity between the nations showed in their open borders and free trade.
cards.why: Enmity is hostility, so shared holidays, full support and open borders all contradict it.

words.meaning: A perfect example of a quality or type
words.note: Greek epitome = an abridgement; the essence of something in a small space.

cards.q: With his tailored suit and perfect manners, he was the ___ of an old-school gentleman.
cards.why: Being the perfect example of a type is being its epitome. Opposite, imitation and enemy all miss the meaning.

cards.q: The tiny shop is the ___ of good service: they remember every customer's name.
cards.why: A perfect example is an epitome. An epitaph is a gravestone inscription, an epithet is a descriptive nickname, an epiphany is a sudden realisation.

idioms.meaning: To be in complete control
idioms.origin: Originally 'rule the roast', the master of the household who presided over meals; later linked to the cockerel in charge of the henhouse.
idioms.caption: Every hen knows who's boss.

cards.q: In that house, the grandmother rules the roost; nothing happens without her approval. She ___.
cards.why: Ruling the roost means having the final say.

cards.q: Though the founder is still chairman, it is the finance head who decides every hire, budget and deal. She ___.
cards.why: Being in real control is ruling the roost. Playing second fiddle is being the subordinate.

idioms.meaning: Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
idioms.origin: A 1700s English phrase, used in hymns for misfortunes that later prove fortunate.
idioms.caption: Bad news. Wrapped good news.

cards.q: Missing the train was a blessing in disguise: it derailed an hour later. Missing it was ___.
o: A careless mistake with serious costs
A lucky break that soon turned sour
A planned move that went perfectly
cards.why: A blessing in disguise looks bad but turns out good.

cards.q: Rejected by every college in the city, she studied abroad on a scholarship and found her true field. The rejections were ___.
o: the straw that broke the camel's back
cards.why: A setback that leads to something good is a blessing in disguise. A Pyrrhic victory is the reverse: a win that costs too much.

words.meaning: To irritate intensely
words.note: Latin exasperare = to roughen, make harsh.

cards.q: His habit of answering every question with another question began to ___ the interviewer.
cards.why: A habit that wears on someone irritates them. Delight, reassure and pleasantly surprise are all positive.

o: The endless passport queue exasperated even the calmest people.
The child's quiet patience exasperated his teacher, who praised him for it.
She was exasperated by the good news and smiled all afternoon long.
Nothing exasperates him more than a calm, pleasant and quiet day off.
cards.why: Exasperate means infuriate, so praise, smiling and enjoying a calm day all contradict it.

words.meaning: Convenient and practical, though possibly improper; a means to an end
words.note: Latin expedire = to free the feet, to make ready.

cards.q: Blaming the intern was ___ for the manager, though everyone knew it was unfair.
cards.why: Convenient but unfair is expedient. Honourable, principled and sincere would not involve blaming an innocent.

cards.q: It was politically ___ to delay the price rise until after the election.
cards.why: Convenient for one's interests is expedient. Expeditious means speedy, expendable means dispensable, experienced means skilled.

words.meaning: To praise enthusiastically
words.note: Latin extollere = to raise up.

cards.q: The brochure ___ the resort's 'pristine beaches', which turned out to be full of plastic.
cards.why: Brochures praise; the irony is that the beaches were dirty. Criticised, concealed and ignored would not need the twist.

cards.q: A nutritionist writes six columns in a month calling millets 'the miracle grain' and urging every family to switch. She ___ millets.
cards.why: Enthusiastic, repeated praise is extolling. Disparages and disdains mean belittle; discards means throws away.

words.meaning: Capable of making mistakes
words.note: Latin fallere = to deceive, as in fallacy and false.

cards.q: Even the best umpires are ___, which is why the review system exists.
cards.why: A review system exists because umpires can err. Infallible and impeccable mean never wrong, invincible means unbeatable.

o: Memory is fallible, so witnesses often disagree about the same event.
The fallible machine has never once made a single error in ten years.
As a fallible leader, he was famous for never making a mistake.
Her fallible judgement was always perfect, without exception.
cards.why: Fallible means able to make mistakes, so never erring and always perfect contradict it.

words.meaning: Changing frequently, especially in loyalties or affections
words.note: Old English ficol = deceitful.

cards.q: Fans are ___: the same crowd that chanted his name booed him a month later.
cards.why: Cheering then booing is changeable loyalty. Loyal, steadfast and consistent all mean unchanging.

o: The weather in the hills is fickle, sunny one minute and pouring the next.
His fickle loyalty to the club has not wavered once in forty years.
She is fickle in her tastes and has eaten the same breakfast since childhood.
The fickle market stayed perfectly steady for a whole decade.
cards.why: Fickle means changeable, so forty years of loyalty, the same breakfast and steady markets all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: To force oneself to do something unpleasant but necessary
idioms.origin: Possibly from soldiers biting on a bullet to endure surgery without anaesthetic.
idioms.caption: It will hurt. Do it anyway.

cards.q: After months of delay, he bit the bullet and told his parents he had failed the year. He ___.
o: Faced a task he had been avoiding
Lied to protect himself from blame
Lost his temper in front of everyone
Gave up and left home for good
cards.why: Biting the bullet is facing something painful you have been putting off.

cards.q: The startup could not afford the losses any longer, so the founder finally shut down its most loved but unprofitable product. She ___.
cards.why: Doing the painful but necessary thing is biting the bullet. Letting sleeping dogs lie is avoiding it.

idioms.meaning: A confused mess, or a supposed discovery that turns out to be worthless
idioms.origin: Since a mare does not build a nest, 'finding a mare's nest' meant getting excited over something that did not exist.
idioms.caption: A great discovery. Of nothing.

cards.q: The reporter's 'scandal' turned out to be a mare's nest: the missing money had simply been filed in the wrong account. It was ___.
o: A real scandal that was covered up
A small story that grew huge
A secret that was never solved
cards.why: A mare's nest is an illusory discovery, or a muddle.

cards.q: Twelve departments, three conflicting rulebooks and no one sure who approves what: the permit process is ___.
cards.why: A hopeless muddle is a mare's nest. A moot point is a question no longer worth debating.

words.meaning: Conspicuously and shamelessly wrong
words.note: Latin flagrare = to blaze, as in conflagration.

cards.q: Building on the riverbed was a ___ violation of the law, visible from the highway.
cards.why: A violation visible from the highway is glaring. Minor, technical and subtle all suggest it was easy to miss.

cards.q: The referee sent him off for a ___ foul in front of the whole stadium.
cards.why: An obvious, shameless foul is flagrant. Fragrant means sweet-smelling, fragmented means broken up, flamboyant means showy.

words.meaning: To stir up trouble or unrest
words.note: Latin fomentum = a warm poultice, from fovere, to heat.

cards.q: He was arrested for spreading rumours meant to ___ violence between the two communities.
cards.why: Rumours meant to cause violence foment it. Prevent and calm do the reverse; report is neutral.

o: Fake videos were shared to foment anger before the election.
She fomented peace by calming both sides and getting them to talk.
The mediator fomented an agreement that everyone was happy with.
His speech fomented calm, sending the crowd quietly home to bed.
cards.why: Foment means stir up trouble, so calming, agreement and a peaceful crowd all contradict it.

words.meaning: Pitifully sad and lonely; (of hope) unlikely to succeed
words.note: Old English forloren = lost, abandoned.

cards.q: A ___ puppy sat in the rain outside the closed shop, waiting for someone who never came.
cards.why: Alone in the rain, waiting in vain, is pitifully sad. Frisky, contented and playful are happy.

cards.q: With the team needing 90 runs off the last over, the fans still waved their flags, though few believed. Their hope was ___.
cards.why: A hope with almost no chance is forlorn. Well-founded, realistic and justified all mean likely to succeed.

words.meaning: Not serious; silly or trivial
words.note: Latin frivolus = silly, worthless.

cards.q: The court dismissed the case as ___, fining the man who sued his neighbour for sneezing too loudly.
cards.why: Suing over a sneeze is silly. Serious, compelling and urgent all mean the case deserved attention.

o: She spent her bonus on frivolous things she never used.
His frivolous essay on war crimes was praised for its grave, careful tone.
The frivolous meeting decided the country's entire defence budget.
In a frivolous mood, the judge solemnly sentenced the accused to life.
cards.why: Frivolous means silly and trivial, so a grave tone, a vital decision and a solemn sentence all contradict it.

words.meaning: Secretive and sly, out of guilt or a wish not to be noticed
words.note: Latin furtum = theft, from fur, thief.

cards.q: He cast a ___ glance at the answer sheet on the next desk.
cards.why: A secret look at someone's answers is furtive. Open, bold and unabashed all mean done without hiding.

cards.q: A man in a cap keeps looking over his shoulder, slips a packet into a bin and walks quickly away without making eye contact. His behaviour is ___.
cards.why: Secretive, guilty-looking behaviour is furtive. Brazen is shameless, flamboyant is showy, ingenuous is innocent.

idioms.meaning: To admit defeat and give up
idioms.origin: From boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop a fight his boxer is losing.
idioms.caption: Into the ring. Fight over.

cards.q: After three failed attempts at the exam, he threw in the towel and joined the family business. He ___.
cards.why: Throwing in the towel means quitting.

cards.q: Facing heavy losses for the fifth year, the airline stopped all flights and filed for closure. It had ___.
cards.why: Giving up is throwing in the towel. Throwing down the gauntlet is the opposite: issuing a challenge.

idioms.meaning: Something bought or accepted without being seen or checked first
idioms.origin: Medieval markets sold piglets in a sack, a poke; a dishonest seller might slip in a cat instead.
idioms.caption: Paid for a pig. Got a cat.

cards.q: Buying a used car online without an inspection is buying a pig in a poke. It means ___.
o: Paying far too much for something
Buying something you do not need
Getting a bargain by sheer luck
cards.why: A pig in a poke is bought sight unseen, with the risk that it is not what was promised.

cards.q: He paid a deposit on a flat from one photograph, without visiting it or checking the papers. He bought ___.
cards.why: Buying without checking is buying a pig in a poke. A white elephant is a costly, useless possession.

words.meaning: Impressive or ambitious in a pompous, exaggerated way
words.note: Italian grandioso = grand.

cards.q: His ___ plan to build a city on the moon by next year impressed no one at the bank.
cards.why: An absurdly ambitious plan is grandiose. Down-to-earth, feasible and sensible all describe realistic plans.

o: The minister made grandiose promises that the budget could never support.
The grandiose wedding was a quiet affair with six guests and a home-cooked meal.
His grandiose ambitions were limited to finishing his homework on time.
Her grandiose office was a small desk in a corner of the kitchen.
cards.why: Grandiose means pompously grand, so a quiet wedding, small ambitions and a corner desk all contradict it.

words.meaning: A person who believes pleasure is the most important thing in life
words.note: Greek hedone = pleasure.

cards.q: He spends his money on fine food, travel and parties, and says he will worry about tomorrow when it comes. He is a ___.
cards.why: Living for pleasure is the mark of a hedonist. A stoic endures, an ascetic denies himself, an abstainer refuses indulgence.

cards.q: The monk and the ___ shared a train compartment: one fasting, the other ordering a third dessert.
cards.why: The contrast with a fasting monk needs a pleasure-seeker. Pilgrim, missionary and scholar do not make the contrast.

words.meaning: A belief or opinion sharply opposed to accepted doctrine
words.note: Greek hairesis = choice; a heretic chooses his own belief.

cards.q: In that office, suggesting a four-day week was treated as ___.
cards.why: An idea treated as shockingly against accepted belief is heresy. Common sense, routine and policy are all accepted.

cards.q: In the Middle Ages, ___ could be punished by burning at the stake.
cards.why: Dissent from church doctrine was heresy. Hearsay is rumour, heredity is inheritance of traits, hierarchy is a ranking.

words.meaning: Unchanging over time; unable to be changed
words.note: Latin in- (not) + mutare (to change), as in mutation.

cards.q: The laws of physics are ___; no court or parliament can repeal gravity.
cards.why: Laws no one can repeal are unchangeable. Negotiable, temporary and flexible all suggest change is possible.

o: For the old judge, some principles were immutable.
The immutable rules were rewritten every week by the new committee.
His immutable opinions changed with every conversation he had.
The menu is immutable and changes daily according to the market.
cards.why: Immutable means unchangeable, so weekly rewrites, shifting opinions and a daily-changing menu all contradict it.

words.meaning: A situation in which no progress is possible; a deadlock
words.note: French impasse = a dead end, a street with no way through.

cards.q: Talks reached an ___ when neither side would move on the price.
cards.why: Neither side moving means a deadlock. Agreement and breakthrough are progress; celebration does not fit.

cards.q: For six months, the union will not accept less than 15 per cent and the management will not offer more than 5. The negotiations are at an ___.
cards.why: A complete deadlock is an impasse. An apex is a peak, an epiphany is a sudden insight, an accord is an agreement.

idioms.idiom: Lead someone up the garden path
idioms.meaning: To deceive or mislead someone
idioms.origin: A 1920s English phrase, perhaps from a seducer leading someone up a secluded path with false promises.
idioms.caption: A pleasant walk. To nowhere.

cards.q: The agent led them up the garden path, promising a flat that did not exist. He ___.
o: Helped them find a better deal
cards.why: Leading someone up the garden path is deliberate deception.

cards.q: For two years the company hinted at a promotion to keep her working late, with no intention of giving it. They ___.
o: led her up the garden path
paid lip service to her ambitions
cards.why: Stringing someone along with false hope is leading them up the garden path. Holding out an olive branch is a peace offer.

idioms.meaning: A little-known competitor who unexpectedly does well
idioms.origin: From 1800s horse racing, for a horse whose form was unknown to the betting public; used by Disraeli in an 1831 novel.
idioms.caption: Nobody bet on him. He won.

cards.q: The unknown candidate from a small town was the dark horse of the election. He was ___.
o: A little-known contender who might win
The favourite whom everyone expected to win
A dishonest candidate with a hidden past
A candidate who quit before the vote
cards.why: A dark horse is an unexpected contender, not a villain.

cards.q: Nobody had heard of the debut film before the festival, yet it walked away with every major award. It was ___.
cards.why: A little-known entrant that surprises everyone is a dark horse. A flash in the pan is a success that does not last.

words.meaning: Unable to be calmed or appeased
words.note: Latin in- (not) + placabilis (easily calmed), as in placate.

cards.q: No apology could soften the ___ critic, who attacked the director in every review.
cards.why: Unmoved by any apology is implacable. Forgiving and lenient are soft; indifferent would not keep attacking.

cards.q: The general was an ___ enemy who never accepted a truce.
cards.why: An enemy who never accepts peace is implacable. Impeccable means flawless, implausible means unbelievable, impalpable means intangible.

words.meaning: Out of place; not in harmony with its surroundings
words.note: Latin in- (not) + congruus (agreeing).

cards.q: A glass skyscraper looked ___ among the ancient temples of the old town.
cards.why: A modern tower among ancient temples is out of place. Harmonious, fitting and appropriate all mean it blends in.

o: His formal suit looked incongruous at the beach party.
The incongruous colours blended perfectly with the room's design.
Her incongruous remark fit the solemn mood of the meeting exactly.
The incongruous new wing matched the old palace in every detail.
cards.why: Incongruous means out of place, so blending perfectly, fitting exactly and matching in every detail all contradict it.

words.meaning: Angry at something perceived as unfair
words.note: Latin indignari = to regard as unworthy.

cards.q: She was ___ when the prize went to the student who had copied her project.
cards.why: Anger at an unfair result is indignation. Grateful and delighted are pleased; indifferent does not care.

cards.q: A passenger with a confirmed ticket is told his seat has been given to an official's relative, and he demands to see the stationmaster. He is ___.
cards.why: Anger at unfair treatment is indignation. Nonchalant and complacent are unbothered; sanguine is optimistic.

words.meaning: Lacking skill; clumsy and incompetent
words.note: Latin ineptus = unsuitable, foolish.

cards.q: The ___ repairman left the tap dripping and the wall flooded.
cards.why: Making things worse shows incompetence. Adept, skilled and deft all mean capable.

cards.q: An ___ handling of the crisis cost the minister his job.
cards.why: Incompetent handling is inept. Inert means motionless, adept means skilled, apt means suitable.

words.meaning: Impossible to satisfy
words.note: Latin in- (not) + satiare (to fill), as in satiate.

cards.q: His ___ appetite for news had him checking his phone every few minutes.
cards.why: An appetite that never ends is insatiable. Modest, fleeting and easily satisfied all mean the opposite.

o: She had an insatiable curiosity and read everything.
His insatiable hunger vanished after a single biscuit.
The insatiable reader was satisfied after one short story.
With insatiable thirst, he took one sip and pushed the glass away.
cards.why: Insatiable means can never be satisfied, so being filled by a biscuit, a story or a sip all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: To avoid becoming too close or friendly with someone
idioms.origin: The picture is of holding someone away with your arm fully stretched out.
idioms.caption: Close enough to talk. No closer.

cards.q: The new manager kept the staff at arm's length, polite but never friendly. He ___.
o: Was rude and hostile to them
cards.why: Keeping someone at arm's length is maintaining distance, without hostility.

cards.q: Knowing the reporter's reputation, the actor answered his questions politely but never invited him home or shared anything personal. He kept him ___.
cards.why: Maintaining a polite distance is keeping someone at arm's length. An ivory tower is detachment from real life.

idioms.meaning: A profound or notable transformation
idioms.origin: From Ariel's song in Shakespeare's The Tempest, describing a drowned man who undergoes 'a sea-change into something rich and strange'.
idioms.caption: Into something rich and strange.

cards.q: The new principal brought a sea change in the school's culture. She brought ___.
cards.why: A sea change is profound transformation, not a small or brief one.

cards.q: Twenty years ago, almost no one in the town paid online; today even the vegetable sellers use QR codes. There has been ___.
cards.why: A sweeping transformation is a sea change. A storm in a teacup is a fuss over nothing.

words.meaning: To grow weak, or to be kept in an unpleasant place or state
words.note: Latin languere = to be faint, as in languid.

cards.q: The bill was allowed to ___ in committee for six years and never became law.
cards.why: Lying neglected for years is languishing. Flourish and prosper mean thrive; advance means move forward.

o: Thousands of undertrials languish in jail awaiting trial.
The plants languished in the rich soil and grew taller every week.
He languished in his new job, winning three promotions in a year.
The project languished, finishing early and well under budget.
cards.why: Languish means weaken or be neglected, so thriving plants, promotions and early completion all contradict it.

words.meaning: Producing a great deal of profit
words.note: Latin lucrum = gain, profit.

cards.q: He left teaching for a more ___ job in banking, though he missed the classroom.
cards.why: 'Though he missed the classroom' implies the new job paid better, not that it was more satisfying. Fulfilling, modest and relaxed miss the money point.

cards.q: The coaching business proved so ___ that he opened twelve branches.
cards.why: Very profitable is lucrative. Ludicrous means absurd, lucid means clear, lugubrious means mournful.

words.meaning: Easily shaped or influenced
words.note: Latin malleus = hammer; metal that can be hammered into shape.

cards.q: Young minds are ___, which is why early teachers matter so much.
cards.why: Easily shaped minds explain why teachers matter. Rigid, obstinate and fixed mean the opposite.

cards.q: Gold can be beaten into a sheet so thin that light passes through it. Gold is highly ___.
cards.why: Metal that can be hammered thin is malleable. Brittle breaks easily, volatile evaporates or changes, impenetrable cannot be got through.

words.meaning: Lacking interest or excitement; ordinary
words.note: Latin mundus = the world: of this world, not of heaven.

cards.q: The spy's real job was surprisingly ___: filing reports and attending budget meetings.
cards.why: Filing and budget meetings are dull routine. Thrilling, glamorous and dangerous are what one would expect of a spy.

o: She escaped the mundane office routine by painting.
The mundane adventure took them across three deserts and a war zone.
His mundane life as a stunt pilot was full of danger every day.
It was a mundane evening of fireworks, music and a surprise wedding.
cards.why: Mundane means dull and ordinary, so desert adventures, daily danger and a surprise wedding all contradict it.

words.meaning: The lowest point
words.note: Arabic nazir as-samt = opposite the zenith. The opposite of zenith.

cards.q: The team reached its ___ when it lost to a club of schoolboys.
cards.why: Losing to schoolboys is the low point. Zenith, peak and prime are all the highest point.

cards.q: A company's shares fall from 900 to 12 in one year before slowly recovering. The price of 12 was its ___.
cards.why: The lowest point is the nadir. A pinnacle is the peak, a threshold is a starting point, a median is a middle value.

idioms.meaning: To be careful to behave politely and properly
idioms.origin: Origin uncertain: perhaps a child learning to tell p from q, or an innkeeper keeping track of pints and quarts.
idioms.caption: Careful now. Best behaviour.

cards.q: Before the dinner with her in-laws, her mother told her to mind her Ps and Qs. She meant ___.
cards.why: Minding your Ps and Qs is watching your manners.

cards.q: Before the visit from the chief justice, the clerks were warned to be on their very best behaviour. They were told to ___.
cards.why: Being careful about manners is minding your Ps and Qs. Biting the bullet is facing something painful.

idioms.idiom: Pull the wool over someone's eyes
idioms.meaning: To deceive someone
idioms.origin: Possibly from the wool wigs once worn by gentlemen: pulled down over the eyes, they left the wearer unable to see.
idioms.caption: Can't see a thing.

cards.q: The fake doctor pulled the wool over the patients' eyes for years. He ___.
cards.why: Pulling the wool over someone's eyes is fooling them.

cards.q: He showed the investors a beautiful factory that belonged to someone else and claimed it as his own. He was ___.
o: pulling the wool over their eyes
throwing down the gauntlet to them
holding out an olive branch to them
cards.why: Deceiving someone is pulling the wool over their eyes. Paying lip service is professing support without acting.

words.meaning: Not well known or hard to understand; to hide
words.note: Latin obscurus = dark.

cards.q: The poem is full of ___ references that only a classics scholar would recognise.
cards.why: References only a scholar would catch are little known. Obvious, familiar and popular all mean widely known.

o: Clouds obscured the moon, and the path went dark.
The obscure singer was famous in every country around the world.
His obscure explanation was clear to every child in the room.
The fog obscured nothing, and every peak was crisp and visible.
cards.why: Obscure means little known, unclear, or hidden, so world fame, total clarity and crisp visibility all contradict it.

words.meaning: Involving heavy effort or responsibility; burdensome
words.note: Latin onus = a burden, as in 'the onus is on you'.

cards.q: The new compliance rules placed an ___ burden on small shops, which needed an accountant just to fill the forms.
cards.why: Needing an accountant for forms is a heavy burden. Trivial, trifling and negligible all mean small.

cards.q: Caring for three generations single-handed was an ___ duty.
cards.why: A heavy, burdensome duty is onerous. Ornate means decorated, ominous means threatening, odorous means smelly.

words.meaning: A model of excellence; a perfect example
words.note: Old Italian paragone = a touchstone for testing gold.

cards.q: The headmaster held up the quiet, hard-working girl as a ___ of discipline.
cards.why: A model held up for others is a paragon. A parody mocks, a paradox contradicts itself, a pariah is an outcast.

cards.q: A judge is never late, never takes a gift and has never had a ruling overturned in thirty years. Colleagues call him a ___ of integrity.
cards.why: A model of excellence is a paragon. A novice is a beginner, a pretender is a fake, a critic finds fault.

words.meaning: A statement or situation that seems contradictory but may be true
words.note: Greek para (against) + doxa (opinion).

cards.q: It is a ___ that the more choices people have, the less happy they often feel.
cards.why: More choice leading to less happiness seems contradictory, yet is true. A certainty is sure, a platitude and a cliché are tired truisms.

cards.q: A city of millions where people say they have never felt more alone. This seeming contradiction is a ___.
cards.why: A situation that seems self-contradictory but is real is a paradox. A euphemism softens, hyperbole exaggerates, a eulogy praises.

words.meaning: To treat someone with apparent kindness that shows a feeling of superiority
words.note: From patron, a powerful protector; patronising imitates the attitude of a superior.

cards.q: The salesman began to ___ her, explaining what a 'gigabyte' was, until she said she was a software engineer.
cards.why: Explaining basics in a superior way is patronising. Respect, consult and appreciate do not imply talking down.

o: Don't patronise me; I understand the risks better than you do.
She patronised her colleagues by treating them as equals in every way.
He patronised the expert by deferring to her deep knowledge.
The patronising teacher believed every student knew more than he did.
cards.why: Patronise means talk down to, so treating as equals, deferring and believing others know more all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: A plan or organisation that is so weak it is likely to collapse
idioms.origin: Playing cards stacked into a tower, which falls if one card is touched.
idioms.caption: Touch one card. Down it all comes.

cards.q: The company's profits were a house of cards, built on loans it could never repay. They were ___.
o: Made up of many small deals
cards.why: A house of cards is an unstable structure that will fall.

cards.q: The scheme paid old investors only with new investors' money, so one month of fewer sign-ups would bring it down. It was ___.
cards.why: A structure on the edge of collapse is a house of cards. A Potemkin village is a fake front of prosperity.

idioms.meaning: To take a less important role than someone else
idioms.origin: In an orchestra, the second violins support the first, who usually carry the melody.
idioms.caption: Always the support, never the lead.

cards.q: After years as the star, he was unwilling to play second fiddle to a younger player. He did not want ___.
cards.why: Playing second fiddle is being in a subordinate role.

cards.q: For ten years, she did most of the research while her famous co-author gave the talks and took the credit. She ___.
o: took the lion's share of credit
cards.why: Taking the lesser role is playing second fiddle. Ruling the roost is the opposite: being in charge.

words.meaning: Not securely held or in position; dangerously uncertain
words.note: Latin precarius = obtained by prayer, so dependent on another's favour.

cards.q: The bus hung in a ___ position, half its wheels over the edge of the ravine.
cards.why: Half over a ravine is dangerously unstable. Stable, secure and comfortable all mean safe.

o: Gig workers live a precarious life, never sure of their income.
The precarious bridge was solid enough for tanks to cross safely.
Her precarious job came with a lifetime guarantee of employment.
His precarious balance on the ladder was as steady as a rock.
cards.why: Precarious means insecure and dangerous, so solid bridges, guaranteed jobs and steady balance all contradict it.

words.meaning: Wastefully extravagant; a person who spends recklessly
words.note: Latin prodigus = lavish. The Prodigal Son of the parable wasted his inheritance.

cards.q: His ___ spending on cars and parties used up the family fortune in five years.
cards.why: Spending a fortune on cars and parties is wasteful. Frugal, prudent and economical are all careful with money.

cards.q: The ___ son returned home penniless after wasting his inheritance.
cards.why: The wasteful son of the parable is prodigal. Prodigious means enormous, a prodigy is a gifted young person, prodding means poking.

words.meaning: To restore friendly relations; to make two things compatible
words.note: Latin reconciliare = to bring together again.

cards.q: It was hard to ___ his generous public image with the way he treated his staff.
cards.why: Making two conflicting pictures fit together is reconciling them. Confuse, advertise and celebrate do not fit.

cards.q: Two brothers who have not spoken in a decade meet at a wedding, talk for hours and agree to start afresh. They have ___.
cards.why: Restoring friendly relations is reconciling. Estranged and diverged mean drifting apart; quarrelled means fought.

words.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulty
words.note: Latin resilire = to leap back.

cards.q: The ___ fishing village rebuilt every home within a year of the cyclone.
cards.why: Rebuilding fast after a disaster shows the ability to bounce back. Fragile, defeated and vulnerable all mean the opposite.

o: Children are often resilient and recover fast from setbacks.
The resilient team collapsed after one defeat and never recovered.
Her resilient spirit was broken for good by the first small failure.
The resilient crop died at the first touch of frost every winter.
cards.why: Resilient means able to bounce back, so collapsing for good, breaking at the first failure and dying at first frost all contradict it.

words.meaning: Relating to the edge; of minor importance
words.note: Greek periphereia = the line round a circle.

cards.q: The debate wasted an hour on ___ issues and never reached the main question.
cards.why: Issues that keep the debate from the main question are of minor importance. Central, crucial and fundamental are the main question.

cards.q: In a murder trial, the defence spends a whole day arguing about the colour of the victim's car, which has nothing to do with the case. The point is ___.
cards.why: A point with no bearing on the case is peripheral. Pivotal and indispensable mean crucial; pertinent means relevant.

idioms.meaning: To hurt oneself by resisting something that cannot be changed
idioms.origin: From the Bible: an ox kicking against the goads, sharp sticks used to drive it, only wounds itself.
idioms.caption: Every kick, another wound.

cards.q: Arguing with the tax office after the deadline was just kicking against the pricks. It was ___.
o: Futile resistance that only hurt himself
A clever way of getting money back
A sensible step he should have taken earlier
cards.why: Kicking against the pricks is useless resistance that only hurts the resister.

cards.q: The old clerk refused to learn the new software for two years, and fell further behind every month. He was ___.
cards.why: Futile resistance that harms oneself is kicking against the pricks. Biting the bullet would be accepting the change.

idioms.idiom: Take the bull by the horns
idioms.meaning: To deal with a difficult situation directly and boldly
idioms.origin: From bullfighting and ranching: seizing a bull by the horns is the most direct, and dangerous, way to control it.
idioms.caption: Straight at the problem.

cards.q: Instead of waiting for complaints, the new mayor took the bull by the horns and closed the polluting factory. She ___.
o: Passed it on to someone else
cards.why: Taking the bull by the horns is facing a problem head-on.

cards.q: Tired of the rumours, the actor called a press conference and answered every question about his past himself. He ___.
o: took the bull by the horns
pulled the wool over their eyes
cards.why: Confronting a problem boldly is taking the bull by the horns. Letting sleeping dogs lie is avoiding it.
